subtopic: SURRENDER BY CANADIAN CITIZENS OF REGISTRATION CERTIFICATES ON ENTERING THE UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SURRENDER BY CANADIAN CITIZENS OF REGISTRATION CERTIFICATES ON ENTERING THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) felt that he was a lawbreaker because he did not have his national registration certificate. I am glad to return to my hon. friend his certificate, thus putting him in good standing in the eyes of the law and allaying any fears that he may have about being picked up by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I am sure that none of us would want that to be done.
I should like to explain to the house, if I may, that an arrangement was made in June, 1943, whereby customs officers at all boundary points and Royal Canadian Mounted Police security officers at seaports collect the registration certificates of persons who are leaving Canada permanently or for more than thirty days. However, the customs officer or whoever picks up the certificate is supposed to give the person a receipt for the certificate, a sample of which I have in my hand. On the back of this receipt appear the following instructions:
Upon returning to Canada the registrant should immediately mail this receipt to the chief registrar for Canada, national registration, Department of Labour, Ottawa, and request delivery or his or her certificate. When writing to the chief registrar please state clearly the address to which the certificate is to be sent.
In addition the traveller is given with his passport a notice explaining why the certificate is being lifted, and I hold in my hand a sample of that notice. The same information as appears on the notice given to the traveller appears on this card which is posted in the border offices. I have in my hand a copy of the card.

subtopic: SURRENDER BY CANADIAN CITIZENS OF REGISTRATION CERTIFICATES ON ENTERING THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
What are the reasons for lifting
the certificate?

subtopic: SURRENDER BY CANADIAN CITIZENS OF REGISTRATION CERTIFICATES ON ENTERING THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I shall come to that in a minute. The notice to each traveller instructs him-I speak now of those leaving the country temporarily-to make application for the return of his certificate to the chief registrar under the national registration regulations, 1940, upon his return to Canada. All certificates are sent to the office of this official in Ottawa, and it was in that official's office that I obtained the hon. gentleman's certificate this morning.
Hon. members will understand that the collection of certificates of persons leaving Canada permanently is done as a safety measure and because such persons naturally would be in possession of better personal identification. The authority for picking up certificates of persons leaving Canada for thirty days or longer is contained in section 28 of the national registration regulations, 1940, which reads as follows:
For the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of these regulations or supplying any deficiency therein, the minister may issue such directions not inconsistent therewith as may be deemed necessary to give effect to these regulations according to their true intent and purpose and any such direction shall have the same force and effect as if enacted in these regulations.
The mam reason, for requesting that direction was a growing epidemic of loss of certificates by registrants and theft of certificates from them when outside of Canada, particularly Canadians visiting in the United States and merchant seamen in foreign ports, both of which are definitely dangerous in war
4S0
Border Crossings

time. Each postmaster in Canada has been notified of this arrangement and instructed to issue a temporary fourteen-day certificate to any returned registrant who applies through his office for the return of his or her certificate. From June, 1943, to date, many thousands of certificates have been picked up and returned under this procedure, with a surprisingly low minimum of complaints or trouble.
Special forms of certificates bearing a full physical description of the registrants are issued to a few officials and others whose duties may require them to leave and return to Canada several times a year. This saves them the necessity of surrendering and obtaining return of their original certificate on each such occasion. I may say that the necessity for this safety measure was thoroughly discussed by my predecessor in office and the legal assistant of the branch with the 'Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the foreign exchange control board, the chief passport officer and others before being decided upon and put into effect.
I now table the form of receipt for the certificate, the notice given to the traveller, the card posted in border point offices, and a copy of the national registration regulations of 1940, as amended to December 31, 1943.

I should like to say also that it takes a jab in the back to get this government to move in connection with anything. This whole thing has served a useful purpose, not only for me personally but in drawing the attention of the public to the situation. I think this is another case of over-regimentation of the civilian population of Canada by this government.

maintopic: MAJOR-GENERAL CHISHOLM REFERENCE TO ADDRESS TO ROTARY CLUB AND TORONTO WELFARE COUNCIL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: MAJOR-GENERAL CHISHOLM REFERENCE TO ADDRESS TO ROTARY CLUB AND TORONTO WELFARE COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) referred to a press report of a statement or an address which had been delivered in Toronto by Major-General Chisholm, director general of medical services. I regret to say that the report would seem to indicate that there was some reflection upon Canadian women in connection with the war. I took the matter up immediately with the director general of medical services and I have his statement which I should like to read to the house. It is as follows:
I regret that the remarks which I made to the Rotary Club in Toronto in a professional address last week-and representing only my own personal views-were misinterpreted as a reflection on the women of Canada.
My theme was the emotional adjustment involved in the transition from civilian to military life and vice versa. I endeavoured to trace these emotional relationships from tribal stages to modern times. It is unfortunate that certain remarks, removed from their context, conveyed impressions which would not have been conveyed had the full text of my address been quoted.
For example, the statement that "in times of stress, such as war, women became a liability" had no reference to the present situation or to the present war, but referred definitely to the women of developing tribes who were unable to fight along with their men when the tribe was threatened. This obviously has no reference to modern times wrherein-in warfare as in peace-women generally are an enormous asset to society.
In so far as references to the present day are concerned, my address was an interpretation of professional findings to an intelligent lay audience. In our professional research we make careful studies and statistical records of cases investigated representing a cross section of the population. Among these are found certain abnormalities, some of wrhich I referred to and described.
It is regretted that the specific cases referred to were given general application to all women in the published report of my address.

Doukhobors
I was deeply concerned about this matter when it came to my attention, and I hope that this statement by General Chisholm will be accepted with the genuine regret which I know he feels that any words of his should be construed as a reflection upon our women folk.
It almost seems to be emphasizing the obvious to try to stress the value of the contribution which the women of Canada make in war, as well as in peace. But in my department we are so conscious of the devotion and the Spartan courage which the women of this country are showing in this time of stress and anxiety that this incident impels me to add a word of my own. Nobody could administer the affairs of the army without knowing that our war activities would have small chance of success if it were not for the fortitude and consecration with which the mothers and wives and sisters and sweethearts of this country encourage their men in the forces and in other tasks of wrar. Here is an extract from a letter written by a mother who acknowledges with thanks the Memorial Cross, which, as she says:
-I received on the anniversary of my son's death. The just pride one feels in being a Silver Cross mother does in some small measure ease the feeling of irreparable loss. David, who W'on the D.F.M. in November 1942, and his commission, was one of three brothers in the air force and one with the navy. One boy has been in Africa since May 1942. A daughter is with No. 15 Hospital in Africa and lately moved on. One boy is in Iceland with a coastal patrol, and one at Victoria. We are the parents of to-day who are looking to a future Canada that will justify the sacrifices being made.
The members of this house know, I am sure, that the spirit of that letter is multiplied in hundreds of thousands of cases across Canada, and I know that they will join me in this simple tribute of grateful appreciation to these noble women of ours whose inspiration challenges every man of us.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEPORTATION OF SONS OF FREEDOM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEPORTATION OF SONS OF FREEDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so that I shall not trespass on the rules of the house I wonder if I may have the consent of hon. members to preface a question to the Prime Minister with a very short statement of facts. On Sunday last, as hon. members may have noticed by the press, more than 400 Doukhobors from my district 100-31
of West Kootenay staged a nude parade. Last Friday they burned a school. Two months ago they burned over $100,000 worth of government buildings. It is a way they have of emphasizing their defiance of Canadian law. Most of the older people, the men and the women, dominate and inspire and influence the younger generation to follow the traditions of this religious sect. Ever since they came to Canada in 1898, every federal government has been unable, and has had to admit the humiliation of being unable, to cope with these Doukhobors. All under forty-five years of age are Canadian citizens. Those over forty-five years of age, with the exception of a few who have been naturalized, have no claim to Canadian citizenship.
My question is this: Will.the Prime Minister, through the hon. Mr. Tounkin, the Soviet ambassador to this country, endeavour to arrange with the Soviet government for participation in the deportation and settlement of these Doukhobors-that is to say, of all members of what is known as the Sons of Freedom, and of all other Doukhobors who violate Canadian laws; and will the government negotiate for the settlement of these people in any portion of the Soviet or in any one of the Soviet republics?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEPORTATION OF SONS OF FREEDOM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has just indicated, Doukhobors who are not citizens of Canada are nationals of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. He has suggested that by conference with the Charge d'Affairs of the U.S.S.R. to Canada I might seek to arrange to have these nationals of the U.S.S.R. deported or repatriated to Russia. May I say to my hon. friend that the question is one of what is practicable. To-day it would not be possible to secure the means of transportation or the means of entry into Russia of Russian nationals who are residing in Canada at the present time. Some other means will have to be adopted of controlling them at least until the war is over.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Finance based on an article appearing in the Orangeville Danner of February 10. The article states that proceedings have been taken by the Guelph branch of the wartime prices and trade board against the

Coal-Orangeville Dealers

firm nf R. D. Bryan & Co., Orangeville fuel dealers, for selling coal above the ceiling price. I quote from the article:
The evidence disclosed that the ceiling price had been broken only when the Toronto suppliers boosted their price 75 cents a ton. When this was done the Bryan Company raised its prices 50 cents a ton, thereby undertaking to absorb one-third of the price increase on its own account, but passing the other 25 cents on to its customers.
The evidence showed that as the Bryans were not importing directly, they were not receiving the dominion coal subsidy of $1.40 a ton, which would have enabled the firm to keep within the ceiling price.
It has been rumoured that the wartime prices and trade board will investigate this case. In the meantime this company, which supply sixty-five per cent of the coal used by the citizens of Orangeville, cannot operate except at a loss, and they have notified their customers and the citizens that they are forced to discontinue business. I would ask the Minister of Finance to investigate this matter immediately and avoid a possible crisis in the fuel supply of Orangeville district.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUESTION OF PRICE OFFERED TO PRODUCERS BY PACKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture relating to the present emergency with respect to fed cattle at Lethbridge which are now ready for market. What steps are being taken to prevent the producer from being compelled to sacrifice these cattle at the "below floor" price at present offered by the packers?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: QUESTION OF PRICE OFFERED TO PRODUCERS BY PACKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provision that is made for the handling of beef cattle was arranged about a year ago. That provision is that there is a floor price under beef and a ceiling price on beef-not on cattle. The ceiling price on beef is set at one level throughout the year. The floor price varies from 2i cents below the ceiling price in the fall to one-quarter of a cent below in the summer. I think the variation at the present time is about three-quarters of a cent. When beef gets down to that price, the board representative of the government purchases the beef and puts it in freezers, freezes it for export to Britain. That is the present arrangement to take care of floor prices in connection with beef. Then there are certain prices which bear a proper relationship, for cattle, to that floor price of beef. My understanding is that in Alberta for about a month's time there has been difficulty in marketing one kind of fed cattle, that is cows; and my information is that there has been considerable improvement in that position recently. The immediate action taken was to examine all the cold storages across Canada that are in proper relationship to killing plants-vegetables, fruits and other commodities have been moved out of storages to take care of some millions of pounds of beef which could be put into those storages- in some of them, now, and in others, very shortly. This arrangement is intended to take care of the situation until such time as sufficient shipping can be secured with which to ship out the meat which has been accumulating in Canada. That is the provision made up to date.

With regard to the first question, whether or not men in "A" category as my hon. friend calls it, are being called, I would point out that there is a difference between being called, that is to say, notified for medical examination, and being enrolled in the army. Requisitions on the Department of Labour by the Department of National Defence are for men of what would be called, under the old classification, "A" category. It may be quite possible that registrars are sending notices to men who are below that category, because they cannot of course determine the category until they come in and are medically examined; but in no cases are we accepting anyone below the equivalent of "B-l" category, which, as my hon. friend knows, is a very high physical category.
With regard to deserters, there are at the present time about 11,000 altogether. I have not the record by district's, but we are getting it. Steps Towards Apprehension
(1)	Inquiries are made locally in areas to *which it is thought the deserter may have proceeded.
(2)	Provost personnel work in close cooperation with provincial and municipal police and the R.C.M.P.
(3)	Provost companies have special apprehension squads to apprehend absentees and deserters.
(4)	Provost personnel may be granted permission to wear plain clothes for the purpose of pursuing their inquiries.
(5)	Where considered desirable the next-of-kin are communicated with and are informed of the consequences of continued absence, and that it will ultimately result in the stoppage of dependents' allowance and assigned pay.
Inquiry sometimes show's that a man has reenlisted in another force, in which case consideration is given to the question of which force he shall continue to serve in.
It is impossible to detail the steps taken in each individual case, since each case presents to some extent a special problem and the answer to which is dependent on the extent to which the community can be expected to assist. The methods used in one case will not produce results in another ease, and methods used in one district will not produce results in another district.
What about the number of absentees?
After eight days they are all deserters.
I asked the minister about those who had not answered the draft call. It would not include those.
That has nothing to do with my department.

There are one or two matters I want to discuss with the minister; they relate to several questions that were brought up last year. One of them, has to do with the first and second items regarding pay and allowances and administration. May I refer the minister to a certain matter that came up in the British House of Commons on December 14 last, when Mr. Anthony Eden, speaking for the government on the Cairo conference, made a statement regarding the commitments of Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the United States in the Pacific in connection with Japan. He said in that debate that while the Pacific being looked upon somewhat as the territory of the United States, which had been looking after that particular work with some assistance, the
Cairo conference had been attended only by Mr. Churchill, Mr. Roosevelt, and the representative of China. He emphasized that the fight with Japan was a fight to the bitter end, whatever the cost might be and howeve' long it might take. I wonder if the peopl of Canada and of Great Britain and of all America are aware of what that will entail in the future, seeing that Russia is not at war with Japan and was not represented at Cairo. That is one matter which I think we should make clear to the people. We should let them know what our commitments will be as to Japan, because even if the war with Germany came to an end, there is no doubt that this other struggle will continue for a considerable time, and we are committed to it on the principle that when Britain is at war Canada is at war; and also we have separately declared war on Japan. We are therefore a belligerent so far as Japan is concerned.
Another question regarding which I should like to get some information from the minister is the matter of embarkation leave, cheaper fares and cheaper meals and berths on trains, better transportation facilities, week-ends in the camps, and the question of bonus, equality of treatment for all ranks and dependents not as a matter of charity.
With regard to the chaplain service, the Lord Archbishop of Huron, who was elected metropolitan of Ontario yesterday, Doctor Seager, made a sensible suggestion recently. At the exhibition camp in Toronto the different branches of the armed services have separate chaplains, and he suggested, as something that would make for economy, that in the larger cities the soldiers should be allowed time off on Sunday morning to attend the church of their own choice instead of one to which they are compelled to go every Sunday. Not only would it be economical but it would be satisfactory to the men themselves. I think that this suggestion should be taken into consideration in revising the regulations with regard to the chaplain service. So far as civilian status goes, the soldier loses all his rights as a citizen once he enlists in the forces. There is no doubt about that. If a soldier is killed the civil authorities cannot hold an inquest. It is prohibited. The soldier cannot even write a letter now. He has to be a major-general to write a letter or make a speech, as was shown yesterday. There seems to be one law for the private and the noncommissioned officer and another law for the other ranks. I am not criticizing the fine officer to whom I referred' last night. I was not able to be here yesterday until very late and did not want to hold up the item. I wish to see the item carry. I do not desire to cast
War Appropriation-Army

any reflection on General Chisholm. He has given his view on leave for soldiers, but he also gave his views last Christmas. He said, in the language of the children, "there ain't no Santa Claus." If he had waited two months and heard the speech from the throne he would have found there was a Santa Claus for every day of the year. I do not believe though that there should be one law for the privates and another law for the other ranks.
I believe there should be better and more holiday leaves and week-end leaves, and there should be no deduction for the time taken travelling from the training centre to the homes of the soldiers. Women are charged $2.05 to go up to Camp Borden and if they have two or three children it takes all the money that the soldier makes in a week to pay the fare. There should be some revision. The railways are making fabulous sums out of this war, and for that reason there should be some reduction in the fares charged the men. When one takes into consideration all the money they are making out of the government surely they can do something to help the soldiers in the camps across Canada. In addition to that, hospital services should be improved and better housing provided.
Mr. Morgenthau, the able treasurer of the United States, went over to Italy last month. When he came back he told a committee of congress what he found there. He said that the soldiers asked him if they were to do the fighting over there in Italy and pay for the war when they came back. He struck out a great many items for home defence. I was surprised to read in the December issue of the report of the National City -bank about the huge reduction in the United States in the home defence items. Hundreds of millions of dollars were cut out of some items. Millions of dollars that appeared in the past fiscal year have not yet been spent and they have been reduced 50 per cent. I appreciate that a home defence army is sometimes necessary, but the camps are filled all over Canada. They are talking about curtailing leave, but some of them from the city of Toronto cannot get home at all as they are in camps all over Canada. A great many in the home defence army could be better employed in industry under selective service, because they are not going overseas. Most of -them are unfit -to go overseas. I believe there should be some reduction.
I am surprised something has not been done about the inequalities in pay. It costs a private just as much for rent, board and food as it does a junior commissioned officer or a senior officer getting $15 or $20 a day. I should think there should be some revision (Mr. Church.]
in so far as selective service is concerned. Nearly three years ago I sent the ministers a copy of the Sparkman bill which was introduced in Washington. My friend from Vancouver South referred to it several times last session, and has taken a great interest in it. I can find no relief along that line at all. Some of the service men will find themselves turned out of their homes on May 1, and -they will not be able to get a house anywhere. I should like to see something done in regard to the housing situation in the city of Toronto. They have been successful to -a certain extent in getting some of these large places converted into apartments for the Wrens and others. I see no reason therefore why the soldiers should be living under such awful conditions as those that exist there at the present time. Counsel should be provided in the law courts for those who get into trouble. I read- in the press that soldiers are appearing in police courts all over the country. Nobody appears for them. An officer may say lie has been a good soldier. Without hearing him at all the accused is sent down. Some of these men are in gaols in the province of Ontario that have been condemned as unfit for civilians. Why should they be used for soldiers.
I have pressed now for four years or more the matter of a national system of insurance for soldiers. If it was successful in the United States in the last war, I am sure it would be successful in Canada. If it were not for the opposition of the insurance companies I believe we would long ago have had a national system of insurance which would take care of unemployment after the war and provide some remuneration for the soldier. I brought this matter up three years ago and it was frowned on by the Minister of Finance. I have also referred to the matter of a records office. I think it is too bad that we cannot obtain from the records office the number of men who have enlisted from the different municipalities in Canada. The municipalities will require that to deal with unemployment after the war. The victory loan people can tell you how much money has been contributed daily by every municipality in Canada. Why can we not cooperate with them and have a similar system of records? I admit the minister has done some good work, but it is almost an impossible task to do it all. I admit he has made some improvement. It is too bad we cannot get this information. Soldiers from all over Canada are enlisting in the city of Toronto. When the war is over they will head for Toronto. Our military district gets no credit for it in the records. The municipal authorities are entitled to know what men have enlisted and their place of

War Appropriation-Army
abode. How can they get that if there is no records office? There is no doubt about the contribution of Canada to the war effort, but I should like to point out that last June I asked the minister if he would give some explanation why, when General Montgomery marched across the desert to meet the American forces, there were no Canadians along with him. The minister was going to reply when the Speaker interrupted him on the orders of the day, saying that it should be put on the order paper, and it was never answered. I believe the people of Canada are entitled to have some information about the Cairo conference. This committee does not know one thing about what happened at Cairo; neither does anyone else in Canada.
Mr. Churchill made changes in British generals in the darkest hour of the war in Africa. General Wavell was transferred, General Auchinlech and General Ritchie were removed, and Generals Montgomery and Alexander were put in charge and then marched nearly 3,000 miles across the desert. There were no Canadians with him. I asked the minister where they were. Were they tied up in the old country? I do not wish to criticize the minister; far from it. I know he is a hard-working minister. I do not wish to bring into the debate anything that is not regular. I believe the people of Canada should know something about it. After all, who is paying for the war? It is the people of Canada. Why should this information be kept in the secret office of some minister and some deputy minister and not given to parliament, as in England?
I have read the debates of the British House of Commons. Last year I sent a copy of the British Hansard to the minister. Major-General Markland, V.C., had returned from the front. He criticized the government of which he is a supporter. Mr. Churchill replied the next day in the house giving a full statement of the facts. I urge the minister to take note of these matters and make a statement on them before the resolution passes. In these days the rights and privileges of the private members are curtailed, so much so that if, under the political system we have in this country, a member rises and criticizes the government, he has not much chance. He is a marked man, if he criticizes it at all, and in so far as any promotion is concerned, it is easier for a camel to get through the eye of a needle than for him to look for any relief or get any information in the house.
The minister, as I have said, is a hard-working man. I hope he will give some attention to the matters I have raised. I trust that he will give relief such as that prvoided by the Sparkman Act, which I proposed three years
ago. I sent a copy of that act to the minister, and my friend from Vancouver South gave an elaborate explanation of it to the house last year.

I shall take into consideration what my hon. friend has said on a number of subjects. I promised him last night that I would see if I could not get him a new comparative statement with regard to pay and allowances and benefits, similar to the one which was furnished last year. I think v.hen I do that, the matter of inequalities in pay, and some other matters to which he has referred, will perhaps appear in a form which would render discussion of them somewhat easier. We will see if inequalities still exist.
I am referring my hon. friend, for the purposes of the record, to a return made to an order of the House of Commons. No. 151, dated March 26, 1942, and I would ask him if that is the form in which he wishes to have a further return and a further comparison and compilation.
My hon. friend, too, has discussed very often the matter of leave. There was one matter I promised last session to take into consideration. I have in mind the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) with regard to reductions in railway fares. A suggestion was made that there should be some sort of ceiling on these fares. What the hon. member probably had in mind was a zone system under which anyone moving m any part of a certain zone would pay a certain flat rate. That did not commend itself to those who were discussing the matter, because it meant that one soldier would really be paying for another soldier's fare. Perhaps I might have misunderstood her suggestion, but arising out of her representation, we have been working with the railway companies-and I cannot say more than that-on a variation of the same idea, to see if there is any possibility of establishing a ceiling for these one-third fare leaves, that is, a maximum above which no soldier would have to pay, regardless of distance. This would mean a contribution by either the railway company or the government toward making up the deficiency created by such underpayment. I say that matter is under discussion, and I may add for the benefit of the hon. member who has just spoken that that is the only thing now under discussion in connection with a reduction in railway fares.
As a matter of fact, as my hon. friend probably knows, in the United States fares are paid by the soldier. There is no contribution made by the government in respect of fares on leave warrants. We are considerably
War Appropriation-Army

ahead of that in Canada, and I think generally speaking the system we have has worked well.
If I understood correctly my hon. friend's suggestion in respect of chaplain services, it was to the effect that instead of there being compulsory church parades the men should be allowed to attend the churches of their choice. Speaking for myself, and having regard to my experience in the last war, I am not so sure whether I would have attended church very often if left to my own volition. As a matter of fact I thought church parade was a pretty good sort of moral and disciplinary measure. At the same time I would say to him that in Toronto, and other places where there are many churches, I am sure a man would have the'right to go to any church he might select, and that compulsory church parades in depots or establishments where there were large numbers of men might be held at certain stated periods. That is so in Ottawa, and I believe ii is so in Toronto. Where there are church parades they are generally just Protestant or Roman Catholic parades. The different Frotestant denominations do not divide up and have different parades.
The matter of housing is a bit out of my bailiwick, but- I am tremendously interested in housing for soldiers' dependents. My hon. friend pointed out that the navy had such housing accommodation in Toronto. I think he must have meant the barracks on the lake shore front. In that respect the army has exactly the same sort of provision in its establishment at the Exhibition grounds, Toronto. Regarding houses for soldiers' dependents, in every case where it has been brought to the attention of the government I have endeavoured to take an interest, and I have been able to get from the wartime housing commission a certain number of houses for the use of municipalities. I refer, of course, to municipalities where wartime housing is taking place. That is the sort of municipality in which there is likely to be a scarcity of houses. We have been able to get from the commission a certain number of houses for the use of such municipalities in order that they may be put at the disposal of soldiers' dependents.
The matter of legal aid has been mentioned. May I at this point express a word of appreciation to the Canadian Bar Association for a very forward and useful step they have taken in providing legal aid for soldiers. Committees have been appointed in the larger towns, and a routine has been established whereby if a man wishes legal assistance he speaks to his commanding officer, or the officer next in charge, and the matter is looked into. Immediately he is put in touch with some member of the Canadian Bar Association who 	'	.	1
has volunteered to do that kind of work. It is something the same as legal aid which is provided in the United Kingdom.
And a very commendable step on the part of the bar association.

I might say-and perhaps this is an advance announcement; it has just been authorized, although I do not think it is yet in orders-that the Canadian Bar Association have offered to go further and provide legal aid for dependents as well. That offer has been accepted by the department. I would expect it to be ratified and the arrangements completed at a meeting to be held shortly by the Canadian Bar Association representatives.
The minister might also add, for the benefit of the public,, that this is a gratuitous service offered by a profession which is often accused of being very mercenary.

I am glad, on behalf of my hon. friend's profession and mine, to add that word. Of course, if a millionaire were to come along and ask for legal aid, I would imagine that in such circumstances an honorarium, let us say, would be accepted.
That is a good term.

My hon. friend is quite right when he says that this is a gratuitous service furnished for those who are not in a position to provide legal aid for themselves, or who do not have the money necessary for that purpose. This is done by men of standing in the profession, who give exactly the-same service in these cases as they would give to their regular clients. As I say, they have been expanding, rather than contracting, in this very worthy and helpful service to men and women of the armed forces.

That is
correct.
Does the soldier who is brought before a civil court have to request the military authorities for legal assistance, or is that provided under K.R. & 0?
Is my hon. friend referring to a criminal case?
Yes, where a soldier gets into trouble, and is apprehended by the civil authorities.

The bar association provision does not deal with criminal cases.

War Appropriation-Army
If the soldier makes a request for legal aid, does he get it?

Well, I cannot tell my hon. friend' there is a system in that respect.
I know that in serious cases that is so. If my hon. friend is referring to the ordinary police court case, then I am not in a position to say what the situation is. I can say however that he would be provided with a soldiers' friend in the person of a member of the service who is a barrister. He would not be provided with a civilian lawyer at the expense of the government.
Does he have to request that?
Yes. In some way information would have to be given to the commanding officer that the assistance is required.

Perhaps I might add a word, because in my own office I have made arrangements for assistance to soldiers in connection with court martials and charges laid in the civil courts. I understand arrangements are being completed whereby a man who needs legal assistance will get it. I refer, of course, to a man who cannot pay. I am glad to add my word of commendation to the legal profession. Many of the members of the bar who are offering their services are veterans of the last war and understand the situation very well. Although they may be busy men, they are glad to assist.
I had intended to take some part in the discussion on this resolution, from the general point of view, but I regret to tell the committee that I do not feel physically capable of entering upon any extended remarks. However, there are a few specific subject matters which I wish to call to the attention of the minister and headquarters. They may require some explanation and perhaps some remedial measures or changes in the future.
There is one matter which I should like to deal with at some length if I were capable, but I just cannot do it. I refer to certain courts martial which were held in my city a few weeks ago. The minister was good enough to order that investigation at my request, but I must express surprise at the outcome. I would point out to the minister that some change is necessary in the methods adopted for the examination of men, similar to the one known to us. I am not going to mention the name of the man or of the officers or of anybody else. The fact would appear to be that there were not enough officers to go round, that the panel of doctors operating at the military district depot in question was small in number, and under the system in vogue, 100-32
I believe it is called the Pulhems system, there were not enough doctors to do the necessary work.
I am afraid that in a desire to get in recruits there was not sufficient attention given to all the medical aspects of this man who had been drafted into the army. The result in the particular case was certainly disastrous. I am not going to attempt to allocate the blame, because I could not possibly read all the evidence. The sad part is that the man left no dependents, and there is no remedy in civil law, because there is no one living who sustained any damage. I suggest that if the authorities have not changed the practice and system, it should be done at once. I understand from a newspaper * report that because of the incidence of the case in question the practice has been changed, and I shall look for specific improvement. This man was inducted into the army and he notified the officer he was diabetic. The officer disregarded the warning and this man was dead within thirty hours. The officer was acquitted. I am not going to refer to this again; I am not asking the minister to do anything, I am only hoping that his officers may draw a lesson from what has happened.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer briefly, and that is the withdrawal from the Canadian army overseas of some 2,000 foresters who were volunteers. The alacrity with which the young men of New Brunswick who were experienced woodsmen acceded to the call of the government to join the forestry corps reflects nothing but credit upon them. I assume that the purpose of this corps was a useful one, that they did useful work overseas and that as the war is not yet won there will be necessity still for cutting timber. This would seem to be so because a large number are still being retained on the other side at that work. I do not think we can make any other assumption.
One day last autumn the men in certain camps in Scotland were paraded1-I cannot vouch for the truth of the report, but I think there is a large element of truth in it- and 2,000 of them were told they would have to come back to Canada. As I understand it, not one man wished to return to this country. However, the 2.000 men were brought to Canada in the fall of 1943 along with their full complement of officers. I suggest to the minister that no matter how meritorious or good the object of this move may have been, it has failed. There has been a useless expenditure of the taxpayers' money, and there is great dissatisfaction over what happened

War Appropriation-Army

among the personnel. They cannot understand why 2,000 of them have been withdrawn from overseas service. They feel that if they were not required in forestry work in Scotland they could have done useful work as auxiliary troops, thus avoiding the necessity of transporting men and women from this side to do that sort of work overseas. That is one of their complaints. However, their main complaint is the manner in which they were used after they came to this country. I want to be frank with the minister and the committee and say that I have not been able to obtain corroborative evidence to support the statements contained in a communication which I received from a non-commissioned officer and from which I intend to quote. This man came back to Canada against his will. I understand he asked for and received his discharge and is now in civilian life. Unfortunately his communication came to me while I was absent from home and I did not see it until the end of January. On December 27 he wrote me, approaching me as the representative of the constituency of York-Sunbury; I received his communication in -that capacity and I now present his position to the committee. This is what he said in the opening paragraph:
As the representative for York-Sunbury I would like to draw to your attention some of the salient facts re the return of a part of the Canadian forestry corps to Canada. To my mind, and I have every reason to believe that this is the opinion of a great majority of the men, we have been given a deal since returning to Canada that the citizens of this country should know about, so that in future men returning to Canada will be used as men who volunteered and went overseas to do their humble part have the right to expect, and which we are sure the vast majority of our citizens expect them to have.
I approach the consideration of this matter on the basis of this man's declaration that they had not been used properly on their return to this country. I continue:
We landed in Canada in October after a good trip, with good food, and so forth, aboard ship. We were entrained for Debert camp. We arrived there around six thirty in the evening to find cold huts, no hot water in the huts and no rations drawn. Mind you, sir, this is a body of nearly two thousand men without rations.
Just imagine that situation!
After a time blankets were drawn and men were detailed-
Mind you, this zombie army in Canada was detailed to have this camp ready for these hungry men coming from an eastern Canadian port late in the day, and when the men came in to the camp they found it cold and empty.
After a time blankets were drawn; men detailed to get fires going. About nine o'clock we were told supper was ready. Personally I
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.1
did not go to the mess hall, as like many more the inner man called long before this and I had gone to the war services canteen and had a good lunch. I might just mention here that officers had -to eat there as well as on the first night.
Of course I do not think that hurt the officers a bit.
We had been split up in strange companies overseas and were more or less unacquainted with the personnel of our company.
He just mentions that in passing.
We were there from Tuesday until Saturday night. During Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday it was as near a mob as one could ever hope to see.
I can visualize the situation of these men, and I call the minister's attention to this:
First you would be called for a parade. No sooner on parade than ordered to return to your huts for further orders. And so it continued the whole time. They were at that time trying to get us broken down from companies to our military district depots. As an example, No. 7 district depot %vas called to parade at 7 a.m. in the drill hall with our blankets to turn in. We were then very much in the way of the various district depots west of military district No. 7. However, by moving us from one corner to another many times the other districts got formed up and moved out; this was around 12.00 noon. We were told then to break off and return at 1 p.m., which we did. From 1 p.m. till
3.30	p.m. we did get our blankets turned in and formed up in formation. We were to move off that evening.
I suggest that there was very bad management on the part of those administering this dispersal.
I have cited this one instance, which is true and can be verified by any man there, as an example of the start we made in Canada. Also to just let you think how the men were feeling after four days of absolute inefficiency from start to finish.
That is the charge of this non-commissioned officer.
Through it all the men were remarkably well behaved and they had far more than their share of grievances.
And now for a brighter side of the picture. We left Debert on Saturday night between 8 and 9 o'clock after four hungry days. We left. I might add, with no regrets, and with a feeling of being badly let down by the powers that be.
We arrived in Fredericton the next morning, and this was a treat; for we were taken right to the depot, given a good breakfast, and by
8.30	a.m. they had us on first parade. From that until 3.30 p.m. we went through the various branches, medical, pay, quartermaster, etc., were given our fourteen day leave and any that could got to their homes that day. Personally my pride returned a good deal to see at least our own depot handled in such a highly efficient manner.
I pause here to say to the minister that I believe the administration officer at No. 7 depot, Fredericton, is a first-class administration officer. I have heard no complaints about

War Appropriation-Army
him. I believe he endeavours to do his level best under circumstances that at times may be very difficult and trying, and I have never heard any complaint against him. I am glad to pay him that tribute.
On our return from leave, we were in Fredericton a week and each day made us forget Debert and appreciate district depot No. 7. We were informed we were going to Sussex, which we did on November 15.
I suppose this is all military routine, but just mark this. In order to get to Fredericton they would have to go through Sussex. Now if they were going to Sussex for dispersal, one would think the business-like thing to do would be to stop at Sussex instead of going on through Sussex to Fredericton and then being brought back to Sussex again. That would have meant a considerable saving of money. He goes on; speaking of the camp at Sussex:
The camp was ready and rations drawn. But imagine our surprise to find not only the maritime and Quebec men there but some from as far west as Winnipeg. Altogether there were between 700 and 800 men.
I call the minister's particular attention to this next statement:
The next morning we were called together and an unsigned document was read to us. I enclose this unsigned document minus paragraphs 6 and 7.
My curiosity is piqued as to what paragraphs 6 and 7 were. I have before me a copy of this unsigned document. It is headed "General Information," and reads:
You have been returned to Canada to assist in increasing the production and export to the United Kingdom of vitally needed lumber.
2.	It is the belief of the government departments concerned that you can probably make the best contribution by returning to lumbering operations, with civilian firms.
Very good. If the conditions were right, that was a proper objective, assuming that the men were needed in Canada.
3.	You may apply for and receive leave of absence without pay-to be known as "forestry leave." If you do this you will have to proceed to such lumbering operations as national selective service officials may direct. National selective service will explain conditions of pay and employment to you and will give consideration to placing you with your former employer, if you so desire, or in the locality for which you express a preference. You will understand that this will not be possible in every case. They will endeavour to secure the most favourable conditions of employment for you.
4.	If you accept forestry leave you remain on the strength of the army but return to work on a temporary civilian basis, taking your own chances in regard to earnings.
Note that, please.
109-32i
You will be given an initial free outfit of outer clothing and footwear as required by your employment. You will, while on such leave cease to draw any army pay and allowances (including dependents' allowance).
Note that. These men are still in the army, but at the same time they are not in the army. They must take' their chances. They are brought back to help the war effort as soldiers. That is my appreciation of the situation, and if I am wrong the minister will correct me. I am simply giving my own interpretation of the position. They are brought back as soldiers, as enlisted volunteers-not draftees, remember-to assist in a vital war effort. But then the army tells them: While you are in the army you will return' to work on a temporary civilian basis, taking your own chances in regard to earnings, and you will be given thus and so.
If you ask for leave.
That is what it says in the "General Information."
I know, but you are not in the army if you ask for leave out of the army and you get civilian pay.
But they were brought back to produce lumber as part of the war effort. This is one of the things they complain of. They say this was done under false pretences.
How does the man's family live until he draws his first civilian pay?

I should like to know. I do not want to get into a row about this thing, and I do not want to be too harsh or rough in my judgment. I am going to leave it to the minister to straighten it out. It goes on:
You will while on such leave cease to draw any army pay and allowances (including dependents' allowance). You will not be eligible for army medical or dental treatment. You will not be eligible for any army pension if killed or incapacitated. You will, however, be subject to the provisions of any provincial compensation act which may apply to your employment.
No thanks to the army for that, because the civilian laws provide for it.
You will have the right to apply for cancellation of your forestry leave to return to army employment.
That, of course, is quite proper.
If you take this you will be placed on such duties as your commanding officer may order.
I ask the minister if that statement which this man says was read to them was put out by the army and under army orders. Then I
War Appropriation-Army

ask him to read to the committee, or hand to me to foe read, sections 6 and 7, which this unsigned document contained but which my correspondent did not enclose to me. I have no doubt what was in it.

What was the date of the
circular?

There is
no date on it; 'but it was read to them. What I have is a mimeographed copy of a typewritten document, with no date on it, headed "General Information," read to these men on parade at camp Sussex the morning after they arrived', which, I gathered from this letter would be November 16. This is his observation with regard to paragraphs 6 and 7:
It appears that paragraphs 6 and 7 must have been too unwholesome even for an unsigned document.
Well, that is his observation.

Your correspondent is
saying that?

Yes.
Well, we went to the selective service men. They were only interested in the lumbering industry and of course had no instructions at that time to handle other occupations. Of course, all forestry leave forms and conditions will be procurable for you if you wish to look into the matter.

When we were reduced to a mere handful of men-
This is still at camp Sussex.

-we were told some had to remain and furnish a guard for the camp during the holiday season. Two N.C.O.'s and twenty-four other ranks were attached to No. 6 employment company for this purpose.

The minister ought to have occasional shake-ups in the administrative staffs, and I would like to be taken as saying that I do not think that applies to our district depot; for I have given myself a certificate of character. And Colonel MacDougall, by the way, is not a supporter of mine.

The minister said his department was never static. I hope that has been true at all times, but I notice that they move more quickly when something happens to arouse their attention. I would like to know what the attitude of the department was towards bringing these men back to Canada. For, believe me, not one of them wanted to come back to Canada. Whether they were right in that point of view I do not know. They were soldiers and had to obey orders. My hon. friend was good enough to say that I could leave the matter until after making further investigation-
Surely.

-and I shall have to do that in connection with two or three matters, particularly of administration. I do want to tell the committee, however, what the situation was with respect to the return of that corps and its employment here. The return of approximately 2,000 men of the Canadian Forestry Corps in the fall of 1943 was the result of communications between the ministry of supply in Great Britain and the ministry of munitions and supply here and the Department of National Defence. The question was where the most timber could be produced. Up to the early summer of 1943 the situation had been that it was better to produce timber in the United Kingdom even though it could not be produced at the same rate, since the stands were very much smaller there than in Canada, particularly on our west coast. It was felt better to produce the timber there and save the shipping that would be required in taking Canadian timber over. It was realized, however, that the operation was not altogether, shall I say, commercially and economically sound because of the small size of the timber there and the smaller number of
(Mr. It, B. Hanson.]
superficial feet which were produced per head under those conditions. Munitions and Supply here considered that the timber supply in Canada required a substantially increased output and they asked that the members of the Canadian Forestry Corps be returned for that purpose.
That was Munitions and Supply?

Yes. The matter was taken up with the appropriate authorities in the United Kingdom, the department of supply there, and it was agreed that this could be done on the condition of fixing a certain number of tons. The timber was counted in tons, as members of the committee know, and it was agreed that a certain number of tons per year should be fixed as the minimum which they hoped Canada could produce. It was under those circumstances that the Department of National Defence expressed willingness to bring back 2,000 men of the Canadian Forestry Corps for the purpose of cutting timber here.
I admit that no complaint could be found with that. I admit that right off.

We realized from the start that there would be difficulty in connection with employing these men and we tried to give them notice well ahead. I am interested in what my hon. friend says with regard to the men being paraded overseas. I know exactly where they were. Several hon. members have visited them over there, and I must confess that I do not think I would like to leave that particular spot myself, because it is a very attractive place.
Will the minister say whether bushmen were picked out?

My hon. friend is anticipating me; however, I can answer the question now. As my hon, friend knows, in these forestry companies there is a considerable percentage of tradesmen, mechanics. These men are used for the purpose of handling not only the saws and machinery but the mechanized transport. I have seen them in the lumbering operations in the United Kingdom. They were employing what, in the presence of some hon. members from British Columbia, I would call the high-line system of lumbering. We do not know very much about that in the east. It is used particularly in connection with larger timber. They had the very best equipment possible. There were a certain number of tradesmen among the men who came here; whether they volunteered to come, as my hon. friend points out,

General
duty men.

General duty men who were not tradesmen in the sense in which one refers to a motor mechanic or a sawyer, for instance, as a tradesman. There was no reason under the terms of their service to ask them to volunteer to come home any more than there would be a reason for asking the men in England to volunteer to go to Italy; that is to say, an order would be issued stating that this was the place to go. They enlisted in the Canadian army for general service. They were put in the forestry corps because they were especially useful there. I cannot tell the committee at this stage whether or not the order was given that they come or whatever attention was paid to the desire of the particular individual. With regard to the reception at Debert, all I can say to my hon. friend at this stage is- and I do not want this to be understood as the last word-that what he says sounds to me like bad staff work. There is usually something to be said on the other side. I happen to know the commanding officer of that particular camp, and I would want to reserve judgment until I had an investigation made, which I assure my hon. friend will be made very quickly. Marsh, of the Department of Labour; Mr. F. E. That sounds as if some attention
was paid to the welfare of these men and that a businesslike attempt was made to find out where they fitted into Canada's lumbering economy.
That is not the point at issue. The point at issue is their physical comfort.

I say that was the next
morning. Whether or not they bad blankets as soon as they arrived or whether they had to get them, I do not know; whether rations were drawn or not is another question. The Canadian army could detail these men for lumbering by companies just as it did in the United Kingdom. They could form any special units they desired. The Canadian army took that authority under an order in council which was passed for that purpose. As a matter of fact, they did not need any order in council at all. What was wanted by the operators in the west, and the eastern operators fell in with them, was that these men would go to them as civilians, work at the same job they had worked at before and be paid civilian pay.

May I ask the minister a question right there. Was it not first suggested by the lumber operators in eastern Canada that they should! take these men as army men and pay all that the army had paid them and all the collateral benefits, and that they refused? They simply would not take them under these circumstances.

I shall come to that. That was the net result in the east and the west, as a matter of fact. The army was prepared to detail these men to go into these different companies and1 operate in the woods. eastern Canada on soldiers' pay and allowances would probably cause dissatisfaction among civilian woods workers because the earnings of civilian workers, generally speaking, were, it was said, less than the pay and allowances of a soldier.

Yes.

And their objective failed

Full consideration. As I have said, the Department of National Defence were not only willing, but were really in favour of doing it. Labour unions.
