The order in council is P.C. 8197, which I have not with me. This authorizes personnel to be detailed for duty or granted forestry leave. I shall have to get the other orders in council with regard to coal-mining leave and other leaves. Perhaps I can give my hon. friend the general details with regard to forestry leave.
Provision is made for grant of leave to personnel of the Canadian forestry corps returned from overseas to return to the lumbering industry for the purpose of increasing the production of Canadian lumber for export to the United Kingdom. The officer commanding No. 1 district headquarters, Canadian forestry corps, and the district officers commanding were authorized to grant such leave for a period not exceeding six months. The same officers may renew such leave for further periods of six months. Leave granted is without pay and allowances of any kind or medical treatment at public expense.
With regard to coal-mining leave, leave may be granted to coal miners for the purpose of
War Appropriation-Army

resuming employment in the coal-mining industry. Personnel granted leave must be employed in the actual production of coal; that is, from face to pithead. Leave may be granted for a period of six months and is renewable for such periods of three months as may be considered advisable. This leave is granted on the authority of national defence headquarters and is without pay and allowances of any kind or medical treatment at public expense.
Provision is made under another order for the return of men to the lumbering industry. Soldiers who are skilled loggers and have had experience in the province of British Columbia may be given leave of absence to return to the lumbering industry in British Columbia. This leave is without pay and allowances of any kind or medical treatment at public expense and is granted on the authority of the general officer commanding in chief or the district officer commanding. Leave may be granted for a period of six months and may be renewed for such periods not exceeding six months as may be considered advisable.
Then there is another provision with regard to leave for the purpose of returning to industry. Application for return of a soldier to war industry must be originated by the employer, who will submit application to the officer commanding the unit in which the soldier is serving. The officer commanding the unit will forward application, together with his recommendation, to the general officer commanding in chief or the district officer commanding, who will submit same to national selective service mobilization board with such recommendations or representations as they may consider necessary. When the board recommends that leave be granted, the general officer commanding in chief or the district officer commanding may grant leave.
In the event that the general officer commanding in chief or the district officer commanding does not concur in the recommendation of the board, the application will be referred to national defence headquarters for decision. Leave granted is without pay and allowances of any kind or medical treatment at public expense and will in no. case exceed six months. Renewal may be granted by the general officer commanding in chief or the district officer commanding after the case has been reviewed by the board.
As my hon. friend knows, the other leaves are compassionate farm leave, compassionate leave without pay, compassionate leave with pay, disembarkation leave, embarkation leave and ordinary leave and furlough. I have not given my hon. friend the number on leave, but I shall endeavour to get that.

Do those rules apply both
to men in the active army and men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act?
I think there is some provision with regard to detailing men for farm leave that provides that only men under the N.R.M.A. may be so detailed.

Is there any provision
whereby a man in eastern Canada who is called up under the N.R.M.A. can be sent to the Pacific coast to work in the shipyards? I believe that has been done.

I cannot remember because there are so many regulations. I do know that there is a provision for detailing men for railway work and perhaps there is a similar provision for war industry. I shall have that looked up. That is not leave really; it is detailed for duty.

What is the provision in
connection with the men who work on the railways?

They are detailed for
duty; it is not leave. I am sorry I have not the order in council if there is one under which provision is made for detailing men to the shipyards. I shall have that looked up to see just what the provision is. The aggregate number of these extended leaves, as I indicated yesterday, is something like 8,000.

How many are NR.M.A.
men?

About 5,000 out of the
8,000.
Where a man is detailed for work on the railway or work in a shipyard, who pays his wages?
The employer.

Does he work as a
soldier or as a civilian.

He is detailed for that
work and is required to stay on that work, as I understand it, under the military regulations, but the actual remuneration is paid by the employer. What I have in mind at the moment is that he gets either the civilian rate or the soldier's rate of pay and allowances, whichever is higher, and the employer reimburses the government. Here is a memorandum on the order in council relating to railway duty:
Under authority of order in council P.C. No 8217, dated 26th October, 1943, N.R.M.A. soldiers having a medical grading lovrer than Pulhemg profile 2222222 as might be spared from their military duties for limited periods

War Appropriation-Army
may be detailed to perform railway duty. Personnel detailed for railway duty shall continue to be credited with their military pay and allowances, including trades pay and dependents' allowances. If the amount payable by the railway companies in respect of the service performed by the soldiers exceeds the amount of the military pay and allowances, the amount of such excess shall be payable to such soldier. This excess will be credited through the paymaster's accounts of the soldier concerned.
The soldiers were detailed as individuals and worked in groups or individually as required by the railway companies.
497 were employed on railway duty as at 22nd December, 1943.
No soldiers are on railway duty at the present time, all personnel having been recalled under instructions.

That really amounts to
providing forced labour for the railway companies.
I am putting no construction on it at all. I say that there is power under the order in council to detail men for railway duty.

These men have to work
for the railway. They have no option.
I am not giving any legal construction to it at all. A soldier having the medical grading may be spared and detailed to perform railway duty.

I wish to follow up the questions a little further. I understand that when these men were performing railway duty in British Columbia they were working under the direction of an army officer, and as the hon. member for Vancouver South suggests, it was in effect forced labour because these men are under army discipline and they cannot refuse to take this kind of work. Furthermore, I am told that they were working longer hours than worked by the ordinary railway employee, that they were working 10 hours a day when in British Columbia at least, the ordinary day is 8 hours. I may not be correct in that, but that is the information I have.
Were they getting higher pay than the railway men?
No, I understand they were getting the pay of the railway man or soldier's pay whichever was the higher.
Was the pay of the soldier including dependents' allowance higher than the pay of the railway man?
I gather it would be.
Then perhaps they could afford to work a little longer.

Would the minister give the committee a comparison of the wages
paid? Where there was a difference between the pay of the soldier and railway pay, was the difference paid by the employer or by the government? In other words, would the soldier's pay be higher when he was drawing soldier's pay than the railway workers' civilian rate? I think we should have that information.

It would depend on what soldier you took. A soldier with four children and drawing dependents' allowance would probably be getting a higher rate of pay than the railway man working beside him. You will have to give me a particular case. I cannot give any general rule.

The department must have figures on that because a certain amount of bookkeeping would have to be done and the bookkeeping would reveal the facts. I remember that a few years ago in this house

I have not heard so much of it lately since most of the members have taken a great interest in labour-when we spoke of low wages the reply was: What about the soldier drawing SI.30 a day? We pointed out then that the soldier at $1.30 a day was getting more than many men in civilian work, and the statement made by the minister just now bears that out. I think we should be given the rates that were paid to soldiers working on the railways.

I have nothing here whereby I could give the comparison my hon, friend asks for, but if I can find any case where we have a statement showing the payroll of the soldier, and what he would get if working on the same job at civilian rates, I shall be glad to give it.
Is it a fact that the position is that some men are given indefinite leave from the army in order to get jobs in the woods?
We were talking about the railways a minute ago. Are we talking about the woods now?
Wait until I finish my question.
I am interrupting to see if my hon. friend is really referring to woods work.
I am going to refer to both.

There are two sets of orders in council relating to woods work, one applying to the Canadian Forestry Corps and the other applying to logging.
War Appropriation-Army
Some of the loggers are given indefinite leave from the army.
Not indefinitely.

Six months leave, and it can be renewed for another six months and so on. And they work like the ordinary logger would work, at his rate of pay and under the same conditions. Another group of men were apparently detailed for work on the railways and in shipbuilding yards, and they were not given leave under the same conditions but were told by the army: You have to go there and work for such and such company. I should like to know why such a difference is made between these different classes of work. I must say that I think the government is treading on very dangerous ground and establishing a dangerous precedent when it supplies forced labour for the railways or shipbuilding companies or for any other private employer. It is coming close to slave labour.
My hon. friend is advocating the conscripting of men to be sent overseas to take part in a war. I suppose he will say that that is forced labour.
That is entirely different.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon. The government has under the National Resources Mobilization Act the power to direct the employment of every individual in Canada, including my hon. friend. The government finds a situation on the railways where labour is needed. Men have been called up under the N.R.M.A., and the government has power to detail men to take part in that work, which is after all a war job. That is all. The government is not treading on dangerous ground.
Why are they not given leave like the men who go logging.
Because they would not go on leave perhaps. That may be the reason. One is a privilege and the other is an obligation. That is the difference.

Does the minister mean to say that some of these soldiers have been given leave of absence and detailed to do work in industry, forestry work and so on, and that the government has no record of the hours of work and the pay they receive?

We have been talking about detailing men for railway work. We have not been talking about men working in the woods, as to which there is a special order in council. I have already said to the hon. member for Vancouver East that I shall see if we have in the department any record

of comparative wages, showing the pay these men would have received if they were getting civilian pay in that enterprise as compared with the pay and allowances they would receive in the army.

The point I am trying to make is that it does not seem to me that it is quite playing ball with the men in the forestry corps if any of them are directed to go to an industry on terms as to wages, hours of labour and so on, of which the government has not full and specific knowledge ; and I wonder why we cannot get that information.

If the government detail them, they detail them to go to work under regulations which the government themselves make, just as they detail them to go and train on a parade ground, or go on manoeuvres, or anything of that kind. They go to work as soldiers, and the government, of course, takes care of the situation as regards how many hours they shall work, and that sort of thing, guarantees them at least the pay and allowances of a soldier, and says that if anybody in that enterprise doing equivalent work is getting more than that, it will see that these men get that additional pay.
Could the minister give the approximate number of soldiers detailed to industry, and the various industries to which they have been detailed?

The last figures I have show that for farm duty there were detailed, at the end of December, 166, the number having gone down from 1,700 on September 30. Of course the work is seasonal and the number required would diminish as winter approached. There were 487 detailed on railway duty as of December 22, but, as I indicated, all those had been recalled on December 29, so that apparently there is none now. I have no figures as to any being detailed for forestry duty.
Were there any other industries to which men were detailed?
No, no others for which they are detailed under order in council.
What about shipbuilding?
I stated to my hon. friend that I would look up the particulars regarding shipbuilding, that I have no information here about that.

While the minister is getting a statement as to the various jobs to which soldiers are detailed I would like to say a few words. I would not like it to be supposed

War Appropriation-Army
that I am in agreement with the remarks of an hon. member suggesting that only recently have members of the house other than those connected with the C.C.F. party become interested in the problems of labour. I do not think the suggestion is called for. Nor is the suggestion that the average soldier is getting more than the average man engaged in industry. If the hon. member who made that statement was really interested and took the trouble to find out what the average soldier gets he would not be so ready to rise in his place pretend that that is the actual state of facts. He would know that a private soldier in the army without dependents receives $1.50 a day, his clothing and his food. It is true that he may also receive a pension if something happens to him. But I suggest that this is very inadequate compensation for the extra risks he takes as a fighting man as compared with men engaged in industry, and I would like to protest against any suggestion that the average fighting man who goes into the army without wife, family or dependents, is being better paid than a similar man in industry. That has been suggested before by the hon. member for Vancouver East, and I protest against it because it is not correct.

The member for Vancouver East did not suggest any of the things which the hon. member for Rosthem has just mentioned. What the member for Vancouver East said, and it is borne out by the statement made in this chamber a moment ago by the Minister of National Defence, is that if these men were detailed to do railway work, they would not do it, because the railways would not pay them enough wages. That is what I said.
That is not what I said.

I think that is what the
minister said.

I beg the hon. member's
pardon. I said, perhaps they would not work on the railways, but I did not give any reason, as to whether the railways would pay them more or less; I do not know.

That is right. They would work on the railways if the railways would pay them a living wage. Not only that, but to-day, if these railway workers go on strike to get better wages, they find themselves in gaol, and under the order in council they are guilty of an offence unless they can prove their innocence. These are facts, and the facts are proved by the order in council which has just been read by the minister.

Would the minister say
what disposition has been made of the young
men who composed university training course No. 1; also, why university course No. 2 is being continued at the present time?

I shall have to look that
up.

Evidently many hon. members are very touchy along political lines. The hon. member for Vancouver' East, when he made his observation with respect to the item under discussion, was absolutely correct in the assumption that the difficulty experienced by the Department of National Defence with respect to detailing men to certain industries in Canada from the services was connected with financial considerations. That is not anyone's imagination; it follows from an analysis which anyone who is reasonable and fair will have to make after listening to the minister's presentation of that question. The men refused to go on the railroad because they would thereby lower their incomes. On the front page of the Ottawa Journal last week it was definitely stated that men detailed from the forestry corps refused to go in the bush at $5.50 a day because it lowered their income in contrast with what they were receiving in the service. Those are not the statements of the hon. member for Vancouver East.
I rise at this time because I note that some hon. members on both sides of this chamber are endeavouring to drive a wedge between the armed services and the industrial workers on the basis of the question we are now discussing, and I believe that action of that kind is a disservice not only to men in the service but to the war effort generally.
At the time the matter was first raised, after listening two or three times to the discussion and having some fair conception of the reasons behind it, members of this group took it upon themselves to make an examination of the question. You cannot examine it by merely picking out the single man who goes in the service or the single man who is employed in industry. Wage rates in this country are computed on the basis of the average income over a given industry, and in many cases this method is not fair, because it includes men in receipt of high salaries as well as those who are drawing $4 a day, and that boosts the average. I believe that anyone who examines the question fairly cannot but arrive at the conclusion that, no matter what industry he investigates, with the present tax structure, what you have left to maintain your family on does not compare very favourably with what those in the service are receiving. No one here has ever intimated that those in the service are getting too much.

War Appropriation-Army
Generally, would the hon. member agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosthem?
No, I would not because it is not a fair premise.

You do not think it is
correct?

No. You cannot take the case of a single man and make your analysis on that basis. You have to take an average family. You are getting concrete evidence this afternoon. When you brought the forestry corps back from England you attempted to detail them to do certain work that is now being done by civilians in the country, and when the men in the service stopped to make an analysis of their position after tax deduction at the end of the month they found they would not have as much in cash as they would have in the service without such deduction. The same thing applies to the railways.
That is not the reason why they are not in the woods.

That is the reason the Ottawa Journal gave a few nights ago as coming from those who were being detailed for that work. The same is true of the mining industry. Hundreds of miners have gone back from the service into that industry because an emergency in fuel was declared. But talk to many of the men who have gone back and they will tell you that after tax deductions they find that they were better off in the service, though they feel they are making the 'best contribution they can to the country.
I do not approach this question from political reasons. I am concerned about having a fair understanding of the position of the taxpayers of Canada who are footing the bill and also making sacrifices. I suggest that it is a wrong attitude for any member to take, to try to play the public against those who are in the service, on the basis of sacrifices. When a man lays down his life for his country he does something that cannot be computed in financial terms. You cannot compensate a man for that; the only compensation in that case is to take care of his dependents properly if they are unfortunate enough to be left without a bread-winner.
Listening to the discussion I am convinced that there should be a revision of the wage rates in the industries affected, where you are trying to detail men back to work. Either that, or the taxing arrangements should be revised to enable the men to maintain the income they had by virtue of the service they were in.
[Mr. Gillis.l
May I inquire of the minister with regard to another category that is out of the services and into essential industries. I refer to the men who have gone back to the mining industry. Three months' leave was given and that was extended to six months if they applied. The question is this. Some of these men, since going out of the service into the industry, have developed disabilities that render them unfit to work underground. I know of one man who has found it difficult to get back to the service, the reason given being that he is unfit. He is not fit for that occupation and he is also unfit for the service, and a decision has been pending for some time. Is there any understanding in that regard?
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that the man contracted some disability after leaving the service and going back into industry?
Yes.
No; there is no provision.
He develops a bronchial condition, for example, and he is not fit for the army nor is he fit for that particular occupation. Where does he fit in?

Pensions and national
health would determine whether or not the disability is attributable to service. It may be a service disability, or it may have had its cause there.
But pensions will not take him until he is back in the service or is discharged.
That is right.

I am interested to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) giving me a lecture on splitting up the Canadian people. Let me read what the hon. member said last night:
I hate to sit back listening to armchair generals who are quite comfortably seated in Canada, prepared to carry on the war until the last worker is killed.
Who is trying to s^t class against class, and person against person? The hon. member suggests that there are people who are ready to sit back here and carry on the war until the last worker is killed. Is he suggesting that other people are not fighting the war as well as the workers and that certain people are ready to take advantage of the workers? Who is trying to create class hatred?

I am prepared to repeat that statement. Since coming into the house I have heard men, on this side particularly, whose only desire was to see everyone in

War Appropriation-Army
Canada that could be picked up sent overseas with a gun in his hand to do the fighting. Most of these fellows have done little fighting during their lifetime, and when you boil it down, who do the actual fighting, the slugging and shooting, in wars? Ninety-five per cent of them are workers or the sons of workers.
I never heard anyone suggest from this side of the house, dealing with the question of conscription, that the bankers and industrialists and people in that category should be conscripted. Certainly I repeat that statement.
I am not going to ask someone to go out and commit suicide unless I am prepared to do the same myself, and I am not going to ask the government of this country to go out and requisition boys and girls unless I am prepared to be requisitioned myself. This is an entirely different matter.
It is raising the question of class-class hatred because of discrimination against a certain class.

When you take the wage rates of the country and juggle them as between the army and those who are in Canada, and classify as saboteurs the working people of the county, who by and large are creating the machinery necessary to carry' on the war- when you classify them as saboteurs and traitors because they try to lift the wage standards of the country against the time when civilians now in uniform will return, what are you doing? After all, they are civilians in uniform. That is what the Canadian army is, a body of sensible men, civilians who are overseas to-day because of the failure of those who had the direction of affairs of the nations in their hands during the last twenty-five years. They' arc civilians who will come back to Canada as civilians, and the standards of living being advocated and fought for by their civilian brothers at home will be the standards that will be available for them when they come back. That is the point with which I am concerned. The point raised by the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) is entirely different. Requisitioning men without giving them an opportunity to say whether they are satisfied to follow that road or not is a serious question. Last night I said I agreed with the government in maintaining that army at home in order to perform essential services. Now that the danger of invasion is over, other arrangements will have to be made, and the policy carried out in the past on that question is one with which I am satisfied. I will not ask sormone to do something that I do not do myeolf
