I do not think the statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South to the effect that young men in our banks and similar institutions are not pulling their full weight in this war should be allowed to go unchallenged. If he followed the statements of our chartered banks he would see that up to fifty per cent of the memberships of their staffs are on active service. The suggestion that these young men are not doing their part in this war is not fair.

I know it is difficult to follow these questions in sequence, but in answer to a question this afternoon the minister said there were some 1,100 deserters from the Canadian army, most of whom are in Canada. While the minister has 'the facts and information before him, would he give us a break-down, if possible, by military districts? fMr. Jackman.]

Yes, I told my hon. friend we were endeavouring to get that. I said last night I would try to get it. It takes quite a while to get the information, and I thought I would give the committee the information I have here. I will get the information.
We should be able to get the information by military districts as to how many are N.R.M.A. men.
We shall do that if we can.

May I ask the minister a question before he leaves the arena. I should like the minister to tell us how many of the 588 men volunteered for bush duty, how many are still in the bush and how many have been returned.
All right.

Mr. Chairman, I dislike rising again, but if the few remarks that I made regarding the question of conscripts did not register with the hon. member for Colchester, that is not my responsibility. I did not say what he said I said.
It sounded like that.

I have not heard anyone in this house suggest the conscription of the bankers and industrialists of this country. The employees of the banks are workers, and are not in the category to which I refer. They have made their contribution one hundred per cent.
I am glad the hon. member apologizes to them.
I am not apologizing to them. It is a misunderstanding of terms.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. The minister said yesterday there were about 5,300 N.R.M.A. men out on extended leave. To-day he has mentioned more N.R.M.A. men who are detailed for duty with different industries. Would he tell us how many there are in the latter class, and how many under each of the headings? Are they operational troops or nonoperational troops? Under which heading do they come?

They are not included in the non-operational troops or in the operational troops. My hon. friend was out when I gave the figures with regard to the troops. I said that the number of soldiers detailed to farm duty on December 1, 1943, was 166. I said that I had no figures of any troops

War Appropriation-Army
being detailed on forestry duty and that in connection with railway duty as of December 22, there were 497 employed, but on December 29 all personnel had been recalled; therefore, the number detailed is very small.
There are some in other industries.
This seems to be exhaustive of those classes in which detailing for duty is provided by order in council-railway, forestry and farming.
Are the N.R.M.A. men on extended leave in the overseas category?
Some are and some are not.
Has the minister figures to show how many are and how many are not?
No, I have not.
I should like to ask the minister if the same opportunity will be given the men to go to the farms this year as was given last year to take part in seeding and harvesting operations.

All I can say to my hon. friend is I do not know of any more acute subject being under consideration by the department. Fortunately it is only February, and I hope that I shall not have to' give consideration to it too soon. Let us get the estimates through first. I assure my hon. friend we always have it in mind and we endeavour to make the best arrangement we can, subject to that old and well-worn phrase which goes something like this, "subject to the exigencies of the service".

I would not like this item to carry now because it is six o'clock and some hon. members might wish to say something further in connection with it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, as a medical man I should like to say a word on behalf of a distinguished member of my profession, whose statement in a recent speech in Toronto seems to have been misunderstood. I thought I might say this in addition to what the minister said this afternoon. As I have been accustomed to reading and listening to scientific addresses I may say that the speech of the
director general of medical services did not perturb me. If he had made this speech before a scientific body, such as a medical society, it would have been regarded as a valuable scientific contribution to our knowledge of the many problems with which medical officers have had to deal when working among our soldiers in this war, into which certain psychological factors have entered. I feel quite sure the director general did not intend to make any reflection upon the mothers who have given their sons, or upon that great body of women who have done and are doing such a splendid and patriotic work.
In view of the many statements which have been made in respect of the maintenance of the morale of our forces overseas, over this long period of battle inactivity, may I say that not a little credit for the favourable situation which obtains was due to our high commissioner for Canada in London, the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, who has just arrived back in Canada. I wish to bid him welcome to his native land, and to pay tribute to the splendid work he has done and is doing as our representative in England. Among his many activities are soldiers' clubs, in London, and an officers' convalescent home which he established at his own expense in Gloucestershire. I am quite sure hon. members would like to associate themselves with me in an expression of appreciation of his and his wife's many and continuing acts of kindness to our forces overseas, which have gone a long way toward relieving them of the nostalgia inevitably felt after years of separation from loved ones at home.

I thank the hon. member for Parkdale for his reference to Major-General Chisholm, and the speech he made. It is difficult for a layman-and my hon. friend appreciates this better than I-to understand the full significance of what is being discussed in a scientific discussion of that kind. I say to my hon. friend and the committee, as I tried to say this afternoon, that I know the last thing Major-General Chisholm would think of doing would be to cast the slightest reflection, or to do otherwise than give the greatest credit to the women of our country in the great work they are doing during this time of war.
It W'as most gracious on the part of the hon. member to refer to the advent of the Right Hon. Vincent Massey. As one who has seen at first hand some of the work Mr. and Mrs. Massey are doing, I wish to join with the hon. member in his expression of appreciation. to them, and to say to hon. members and the country generally that I do not think Canada can ever fully realize or recognize not only the fine service these two gracious people
War Appropriation-Army

are rendering, but the devotion and the genuine consecration they have shown in their heavy task for Canada, which, because of the activities of this war, has increased tenfold.

I was glad to hear the minister say this afternoon that the matter of the transportation of the armed forces is under consideration, and I hope that the suggestions made may be carried out.
I should like also to thank the minister for the observations and appreciation he has recorded respecting women in uniform. I believe people throughout Canada would subscribe to what he has said. So far as I have talked to members of different units, and to civilians in our different cities, I have gained the impression that the opinion respecting women in uniform is very high indeed.
Has the minister considered the suggestion that women should have representation on the committees being set up for the reestablishment of troops returning from overseas? I suggest that women should be on such committees which would deal with the reestablishment of women who have been in the services. And I do not think it would be a bad idea to have a woman or two on the general reestablishment committee for all troops, men and women combined.
I was pleased to hear the explanation made respecting Major-General Chisholm's address. I knew it was not meant the way a reading of it might indicate, and I was convinced that there must have been some misinterpretation; because everyone knows that, although there are a few who might be emotionally too sensitive and therefore might upset the boys returning home, the fact remains that the great majority of women have added to the morale of our troops, in every respect. The minister himself expressed his realization of that fact when he referred to the letters received by the men overseas. I am sure a great percentage of that mail comes from the women of our land. The minister referred to that mail as a morale builder for our troops overseas. I am sure that the women of Canada are glad to have heard the explanation, and that they will continue to play their part, one which in some respects is very difficult, during this time of war.

With regard to the membership on the rehabilitation committee, to which the hon. member has referred, possibly she knows that in the Department of Pensions and National Health, over which my colleague presides, there has been set up a special rehabilitation committee to deal with the rehabilitation of women in the services. In addition to that, I am informed by my colleague it is anticipated that there will be

appointed, near the fountainhead of the administration, an executive assistant in the person. of a w'oman, who will work with the assistant deputy minister who is also the director of rehabilitation in the Department of Pensions and National Health. So that I am sure women will be fully represented. The hon. member has a right to ask whether the same thing will apply in respect of these committees about which I have spoken. I can say to her that so far as the army is concerned-and I have not consulted my colleagues in the navy and air force-arrangements will be made so that representation will be given on the administrative body we are setting up for that purpose.

The minister said yesterday there was to be some reduction in the paid personnel. of the reserve army. I understand there are a certain number of men in each unit who are on a full-time basis. Did that recommendation for a reduction in paid personnel come from the units themselves, or is it just a move by headquarters? I am asking that because, particularly in coastal brigades, which are the most likely to see active service, it would seem to be a mistake to cut down on their paid personnel. Has any consideration been given to having the reserve army take over some of the functions of the other troops -perhaps some operational role, such as antiaircraft protection. There may be other work which they could do, and in this way they would enable the minister to reduce the number of men in Canada of the active force.
Mr. RALSTON; With regard to the first question, I am sorry I cannot tell my hon. friend whether or not the recommendation came direct from the units. I refer to the change-over whereby more responsibility for training will be put upon officers of the reserve units, and less by way of paid personnel. The recommendation was made in conjunction with the director general of the reserve army. I know that he has travelled from coast t'o coast, and back again as far as that goes, consulting those who have to do with the reserve army units. That recommendation is the result of that trip and of the consideration which Major-General Phelan, the director general of the reserve army, has given to the matter.
The point is, as I endeavoured to point out on Friday, that with these two years of intensive training-I really think the reserve units will agree with this-it is felt that the officers and non-commissioned officers have become sufficiently trained to take on a greater responsibility for the training of the units. I have not said that the staffs would be cut

War Appropriation-Army
out -completely, but they certainly will be reduced. I think there is a justification for that, and it will give them a little more in the way of self-dependence, in the way of running their own show, which will be all for the good of the service.
The other question was in connection with having them take over some of the work of the active units. That has been under consideration, and it is simply a case of the difficulty of making practical arrangements. Obviously you cannot send a reserve unit from Toronto or Winnipeg to the coast; you could use only a unit located in the area which is represented by my hon. friend and in which he lives. There have been discussions with regard to this. As a matter of fact, I did say last year that I anticipated there would be some taking over of antiaircraft work by some of the reserve units. That has not been carried out to any extent because it means you would have personnel in your anti-aircraft unit who were working in the day time. In these days it is sometimes difficult for businessmen to make arrangements to undertake, say a three months' tour of duty in order to serve on special coast defence duty. The men are prepared to do so if the necessity arises, but to have a unit serve as a whole could not be done advantageously without great sacrifice which perhaps is not required.

What are the plans for the
Pacific coast militia rangers? Units of this corps have been established mainly in the smaller centres and they have done excellent work. I think they would be of great use even in peace time. A few months ago there was some talk about the number of men and the number of units being reduced, and I should like the minister to tell us what he has in mind.

I had a memorandum the other day with regard to the Pacific coast rangers. There is no intention of disbanding them. There has been a certain curtailment, not so much m connection with their activities as in connection with their spheres of activities. As my hon. friend knows, they were perhaps one of the most rapidly growing and vigorous military organizations that we have had in Canada. As my hon. friend says, they have done grand work and they are entitled to full credit. At the same time they did overlap to some extent with the reserve army.
Only in a few places.

I said to some extent.
Of course it is desirable to prevent that overlapping and to decrease, at least to that degree. I cannot give my hon. friend any particulars at the moment with regard to localities, units or what reductions there will be, but the force will be maintained as a force.

I believe they have only
partial equipment at the present time, and I should like to know if they are to be provided with more equipment.

I am afraid I cannot speak with any degree of certainty with regard to that. The clothing and equipment provided consists of a steel helmet, waterproof jacket and trousers, arm band, a -3030 Winchester rifle or a -303 Ross rifle, Sten guns and pistols for the officers. We are not providing transport or other equipment.
Are they provided with boots?
No.
Why not?

We may as well go through all the lists of clothing. They are not supplied with a number of things provided for the regular troops. The jackets and trousers were an extra issue, and the steel helmet was an extra issue. Some arms were not provided, but we have gone a long distance in this respect. I presume that the reason more equipment is not considered essential is due to the fact that they have combined some of the work being done on the Pacific coast with their civilian work. The strength as of December 31, 1943, was over 12,000. The reduction we are planning, which my hon. friend will see is a small one, will bring the strength down to something like 10,000. That reduction will be effective in the same way as the reduction of the reserve army, that is by stream-lining or cutting out the dormant units but not by disbandment.
I think it would be helpful if these men were able to get more gasoline for their transportation. I believe their efficiency would be increased.
We endeavoured to get more gasoline for the motor-boat squadrons at Vancouver and Victoria, but we were not so successful. I do not want to hold out too much hope.

I was interested in what the minister said this afternoon about the No. 1 army course. May I take it that it is the intention now to permit those who pass this course successfully to proceed along the lines of the technical training they have received. The minister may remember that in
War Appropriation-Army

I admit to my hon. friend that the statement I put on record this afternoon is a little involved. I mean, one must read it quite carefully. The first thing, as I understand it, is that all the successful candidates will be permitted to proceed to the officers' selection and appraisal centre at Brockville, under special quota for appraisal by that board. That board decides who are likely to make potential officers, and the personnel selected as officer material will be given an opportunity of proceeding to O.T.C. upon completion of their corps training. This corps training would take probably two months at least. They will be fully informed at the officer selection and appraisal centre of the time element involved in completing officer training and subsequent dispatch overseas. That perhaps is somewhat of a deterrent to them, the fact that if they take the officer training course it may be some time before they get overseas. Selected candidates who, because of the time element involved in the attainment of a commission, might not want to wait will be allowed the option of entering the reinforcement stream as other ranks and of proceeding overseas as early as possible upon 
completion of corps training. They will not be retained in Canada as assistant instructors. Their documents showing that they had so elected will be clearly marked at officer selection and appraisal centre. My hon. friend's question I think would come in there, and the answer is not given in that paragraph which I have just summarized. He was asking if they would be retained for specialist work for which they had been particularly trained in the course. The answer to that does not appear plainly in that paragraph. But the next paragraph of this memorandum does indicate that personnel not selected as officer material will be considered for technical or specialist training such as survey, radio direction finding, signals, and so forth, and be given an opportunity, if selected, of commencing such specialist training forthwith.
Personnel considered to be unsuitable will be immediately returned to the reinforcement stream and dispatched overseas upon completion of corps training. They will not be held as assistant instructors during the progress of training. I should like to have a little more information on one point, whether selected candidates who decide not to wait for the Brockville training but want to go overseas have any preemption on technical or specialist units. I shall get that information for my hon. friend.

I wish to make a few observations with reference to the resolution now before the committee. I should like first of all to say how glad I am that the minister made the remarks he did yesterday, addressed to the Canadian people, warning them that the war is not yet finished by a long way and that a difficult and bloody path lies ahead. It seems to me that the whole psychology of the allied governments has to some extent been at fault in this regard. By that I mean such things as the optimistic statements made around the New Year to the effect that 1944 might see the end of the war in Europe. A number of other circumstances arising about the same time all helped to give the feeling not only among civilians but even among service personnel that we are now coasting into the home stretch. There were, fo- instance, the announcement that the reserve army was going to cut down the number of days training, the announcement that the air force would no longer accept recruits for the women's division, the fact that in some training centres across Canada the number of persons to be trained is to be greatly reduced, the number of officers who are being dismissed from the service-I know men who have come to me during the last

War Appropriation-Army
three months, men in the armed services, who are already making plans for going back to civilian life because of the impression that seems to have been created that it is now a matter of months before the war is over- all these things have tended to give that impression. I think that is bad psychology.
I think the speech from the throne-I am not going to discuss it now, Mr. Chairman- after a merely cursory statement that the winning of the war is the first objective, failed to set out a single particular in which we could improve our war effort or step it up. That also helped to give the impression that we are now passed the peak and are coasting to the home base. The result is that we are psychologically unprepared, I think, for the terrific sacrifices and terrific casualties that may suddenly be catapulted on the Canadian people.
I wish to commend the minister for the very frank statement he made yesterday. I think also that anybody who listened to his statement of last Friday regarding his visit to the troops must have been touched not only by his evident sincerity but by the inspiration he gained from visiting the men engaged1 in actual combat.
I should like to say something about the large body of non-operational troops in Canada. There are in Canada some 75,000 non-operational troops, if I remember the minister's figures; that is, men who are mostly on administrative or training staffs. It seems to me that this is a very high figure. Last year, if I remember correctly we had about
88.000	in A. and T. staffs, while this year it is from 70,000 to 75,000. But 75,000 seems to be a very large percentage of administrative and training personnel to carry. Can the minister in the course of this discussion tell us whether the time has not come to reduce the large administrative and training staffs?
I should also like him to tell the committee how many men are going through these training centres. If I am not incorrectly informed, in some training centres the number of men carrying on administrative work and training actually exceeds the number of men being trained in the camp.
There are about 23,000 men carrying on administration and training for about 75,000 personnel in the training stream.
I did not mean in toto but was speaking of particular camps. I should like to know how many men are going through each of these camps each month. In the province of Saskatchewan-
Maple Creek, for instance?
At Maple Creek in January the number of men who came in to be trained was so small that I would hesitate to quote it.

My hon. friend is right
about that. I was speaking about the camps as a whole.

I am wondering how many other camps are similar to Maple Creek and whether the large nonoperational Staff could not be reduced and these men used to better advantage elsewhere.
I wish to say a word about the large operational personnel. I agree with my desk-mate the hon, member for Cape Breton South, in what he said last night, that last year and the year before there was a demand among the members of this house that the government Should do something to protect our coasts and that therefore the government is not to be blamed for having a large body of men occupied in doing just that. But it may be that the time has come when we no longer need from 60,000 to 70,000 men in the classification of iN.R.MA. personnel, and that something else may have to be done with them. The minister has stated that they will be available for reinforcements. That is true. In the meantime I think the government has to decide whether there is not some better use that cdn be made of them until they are required as second-line reinforcements; that is, if the government is not anxious to use them in actual combat. It seems to me that many of these men who have been already trained might be returned to farms; some of them might be returned to coal mining and forestry. All these trained men could very easily be brought back into units if the government decided that they were going to make some use of them. The time has come when the question of the disposal of these sixty thousand or seventy thousand non-operational personnel should be reconsidered by the government with a view to deciding whether they are making the best possible use of these men. I do not feel at all satisfied with the minister's statement this afternoon.
As to seeding leave for the men of the National Resources Mobilization Act personnel, I do not know whether the minister realizes how serious the situation is. On the prairies there are thousands of farms where the only persons operating a farm are an elderly man and his wife. These people are four years older than they were when the war started. Many of them will not be able to put in a crop this spring unless some member of the family now in the armed forces comes home and helps them1, or unless they can hire help, which at the present time is virtually
War Appropriation-Army

impossible. I think the government will have to give some thought to this matter, and not leave it until April and then, make some hastily-concocted scheme. They ought to be giving some consideration now to two things: first, to make it possible for the men who are from farms to return to them in the spring to help put in the crop; and, second, to assist men who are in. the National Resources Mobilization. Act personnel to be placed on farms so as to assist farmers in putting in a crop this coming spring. I ask the minister to give some thought to that and to be prepared to have a discussion in the house, not at the end of March or April, when- the men should already be on the farms, but sometime during the present month of February.
I should like to ask the minister about the order in council which forbids men in the armed forces taking any part in public discussions, which forbids them writing letters to the newspapers, which forbids them speaking at any kind of public meeting. I think we have gone a long way in this country when a member of the provincial legislature who is a member of His Majesty's forces is forbidden to speak on a Sunday afternoon to an open forum, where he. was asked to go and speak on post-war reconstruction, a subject in which I think most hon. members, and many men who are in the armed forces, are interested. Here is a man who receives such an invitation, accepts it, and then finds the day before that he cannot go and take part in this discussion because, in order to do so, he must submit the manuscript to a national defence headquarters here in Ottawa.
In this country we have never believed in a professional army. Our armed forces have been civilian armies, and we have tried to make them as democratic as possible; we have tried to encourage the fostering of discussion and the exchange of points of view; and I do not think the Canadian people, and least of all the men in the services, take very kindly to the proposition, that because a man is now a member of His Majesty's forces he is not to be allowed to write a letter to the paper, or to go to a public meeting and there express whatever point of view he may have on any subject under discussion. I should like to have the minister in the course of his discussion tell us the terms of that order in council and the exact reason why the government thought it necessary to pass it.
I wish also to say a word about the fact that men who joined the Canadian army from the reserve army and were brought in under general order 139 are not being paid a clothing allowance. There was a reason for that when

that regulation was originally passed. If a man came into the army through the reserve under general order 139, it was understood that he would be in for only a short time, probably to do some temporary task, so that when he was let out of the army his clothes would still fit him and still be in a fairly good state of repair, and he would need no clothing allowance. But the men who have gone into the army through general order 139 and who are now being discharged are men who have been in the army in some cases for three or four years, and when these men are discharged without a clothing allowance they are under serious hardship.
When. I was in the city of Prince Albert, represented by the Prime Minister, a number of men, thirteen, I believe, came to my hotel room. All of them were being discharged on the following Monday. Most of them, I think, had joined up at Yorkton. They did not know anything about recruiting stations, in the early days of the war. They had gone to reserve army headquarters, and reserve army headquarters made arrangements for them to be taken in and sent them straight to Dundurn, and actually, although they had not been members of the reserve force, they came in through the reserve force under general order 139, I do not know why. That is the modus operandi. What is the result? These men have been cooks and batmen and working in training centres. Now, nearly four years later, when they are discharged, they find that there is to be no clothing allowance. They do not know where their clothes are. These men now have to go out and spend sixty, seventy or one hundred dollars to buy clothing so that they can return home. I do not suppose that this incident is typical of the cases of large numbers of men, but it is a serious hardship to the men who are affected.
I should like to make another suggestion to the minister, although I am not sure whether his department or the department of pensions is the more vitally concerned. The department ought to give some thought not only to the question of demobilization of the men coming back, but to the question of the soldiers' wives and the whole matter of the psychological adjustment of men returning after the war. A number of soldiers' wives have spoken to me about it. They point out that when their men come back after being away three, four or five years, many of them come back changed. They have been through a variety of experiences, have come back tired, moody and nervous. Many of these men were married probably only a matter of months prior to going overseas. In cases where the

War Appropriation-Army
wives are young they are at a complete loss to understand the change of attitude and the change of personality that have resulted from years of service. I believe great work could be undertaken by one of the departments of government putting out literature, particularly to soldiers' wives, to make them aware of the fact that any man who has spent some time overseas in service will come back a different person to some extent, and that there is need of a period of psychological readjustment if we are not to have matrimonial wrecks all over this country in the post-war period.
There is one other question which I wish to ask the minister. Will he elaborate to the committee some of the reasons for breaking up the Canadian army? I believe there was a strong feeling throughout the country, and certainly there was a strong feeling in some parts of this house, expressed repeatedly during the past two or three years, that the Canadian army should be retained as a unit. Those who have read the memoirs of David Lloyd George or of Sir Robert Borden, who was Prime Minister of Canada during the last war, will remember the tremendous pressure which was brought to bear upon the Canadian government and the Canadian military authorities to break up the Canadian army of 1914-18, a pressure which Sir Arthur Currie resisted so strongly, and which was resisted by Sir Sam Hughes and Sir Robert Borden. Most historians who have studied the history of the last war have generally agreed that these men were right in resisting the pressure of the British government and the British general staff and in refusing to break up the Canadian army during the last war. That does not mean that it is right not to break it up during this war.
Will my hon. friend elaborate that? There was no Canadian army in the last war, but a Canadian corps.
Yes.
Does he mean pressure to break up the Canadian corps?
In the last war, yes.
I know the fifth division was broken up.

The minister will remember that there was terrific pressure, according to the memoirs to which I have referred, in the early stages of the last war to split up the Canadian corps and to use one battalion in one division and another battalion elsewhere throughout the British army as 100-33
shock troops, and he will remember the fight which Sir Arthur Currie and the Canadian government-
The Canadian corps was formed when there were two divisions.

Yes; but the fact is that pressure was brought to bear to break it up so that it would not operate as a corps but that the respective battalions would operate as parts of the British army to be used as shock troops under the British command. The Canadian government and the Canadian military authorities at that time strongly resisted that pressure, and we have felt during this war that there was a strong demand in this country, and a strong feeling in the army itself, that the Canadian army be allowed to do the better job it could do if it were possible to retain it as a unit operating under a Canadian commander in the field. The government, for some reason or other, has decided to accede to the request that it be broken up. One corps will be sent to Italy; the other corps will remain in England with an army headquarters, and I imagine a British corps or some other corps will operate with that corps under Canadian army headquarters.
Whose request was it that the Canadian army be broken up? The hon. member said that the government had decided to accede to the request that the Canadian army be broken up.
I take it for granted that it was the request of the British government.

My hon. friend can take it for granted it was nothing of the kind. I have said, in my statement to the house, that the government itself of its own initiative asked for a division to go to Italy, and then pressed for another division to go. There was no request of any kind or description by the British that the two divisions should go to Italy. I have said all that. I went into the details of it.

I heard the
minister's speech.
My hon. friend did not listen, I am afraid.

May I hear
the minister again?

I say I am afraid my hon. friend did not listen, if he makes the statement that we acceded to a request and says that the request was that of the British government.

War Appropriation-Army
I hardly take it from the minister that the Canadian government decided to send a division without any prior consultation with the British government.
Certainly we had prior consultation with the British government, but we had no request from the British government. It was on our initiative and not on theirs.

Then the
responsibility lies squarely with the Canadian government?
Absolutely.

The Canadian government decided that the Canadian army, instead of operating as a unit, first of all a division and now a corps, would be sent to Italy and that corps would operate under a British army commander and that the other corps would remain in Great Britain under Canadian army headquarters, to which will probably be added a British corps or some other corps to complete that army operating under Canadian army headquarters.
I do not wish to discuss the question of General McNaughton, in view of what the Prime Minister said yesterday, but I think it was a mistake that the announcement regarding the break-up of the Canadian army as a unit coincided closely with the announcement of General McNaughton's resignation. Also it reminded many people of the fact that after Dunkirk, General McNaughton was quoted by some United States papers as saying that after what he had seen in France he would be opposed to having the Canadian army broken up. I do not mean that that is still his point of view; I do not know. But the inference drawn by a great many people, both inside and outside the armed forces, was that there had been here a distinct cleavage of opinion as to whether the Canadian forces should go into action as a unit or should be broken up and operated on several fronts as different army corps. After listening carefully to the minister on Friday last, the only reason I could gather for the advantage of breaking up the Canadian army was to gain battle experience. There is a great deal of merit in that argument. I ?an see the difficulty in keeping a large body of men in England, the danger of men going stale, and the desire on the part of highly trained men to acquire some battle experience. The minister has not explained why it was not possible to use the entire Canadian army in Italy so as to enable them to remain as a unit. There may be strategic reasons which he cannot give, but I think the minister will have to remember that
(Mr. Ralston.]
there are many people in this country who were naturally anxious that the Canadian army should have been kept as a unit and who will want some further explanation as to why it has not been kept together.
Everyone I believe recognizes that in a unified united nations' strategy all the different countries participating will have to fit into a general plan. That is inevitable, and neither Canada nor any other country can have sole control of the military strategy that will dominate the war effort of the united nations. At the same time the Canadian people have placed hundreds of thousands of their sons in the care of the government and particularly of the Minister of National Defence, and they will want to know just to what extent the strategy and the battle operations to be followed are in any way influenced or affected by the Canadian general staff and by the Canadian government.
I know there are limitations; I know the larger picture will have to dominate. But I say frankly to the minister that there is a strong feeling in some quarters, which may be justifiable-in fact it is there-that the control has been going increasingly into the hands of professional soldiers; that the R.M.C. men particularly, and naturally, since they are the trained men, have been given positions of responsibility; that civilian soldiers have been to some extent pushed aside; that the entire control of the strategy is increasingly in the hands of the British general staff and British generals; and that less and less of the say as to what will be done with the Canadian forces is being left in the hands of the Canadian command and the Canadian authorities. I think the minister could do a great deal to alleviate some of that feeling by giving to this committee, if not now, whenever he can, a picture as to just how the Canadian corps will integrate into the picture in Italy, how the Canadian corps and army headquarters will integrate into the picture in Europe and what consultation there will be with Canadian rpilitary authorities..
For instance, the Canadian people have not forgotten that on several occasions in the last war, if the histories that have been written are correct, Sir Arthur Currie insisted before certain battle operations took place that certain artillery support and certain conditions must obtain before Canadians would take part in the operations that were proposed. I think the Canadian people in the final analysis would be glad to know that the control and the decisions affecting the lives of the men they have sent overseas will be safeguarded

War Appropriation-Army
and protected not only by the Canadian government but by Canadian commanders responsible to the Canadian government.

I think I might as well deal now with what my hon. friend has said.
I have already spoken with regard to some of these matters, and I do not want to indicate that I have any hesitation whatever about discussing the question. My hon. friend has spoken of several comparatively minor matters to which I shall refer only briefly. I have already given the committee a very full statement with regard to the employment of nonoperational troops and their different roles. I can give the committee a full schedule of all the different groups of units which are involved, but at the moment I do not think it is necessary to load up Hansard. Suffice it to say we have a committee, and it is a hard-boiled committee. It is a committee that those connected with the various units in the non-operational group consider pretty tough. They are travelling back and forth in this country all the time examining into the establishments at the different centres, and at the different headquarters as well, in an endeavour to check and see whether a man can be spared here or there. A great many war establishments have been cut down as a result of the action of that committee-not always; sometimes they have been increased. But I wish to assure this committee that there has been and there is vigilance in connection with the matter of the conservation of man-power and every effort is made to prevent them from getting into the backwater of non-operational troops unless they are doing an actual job.
I have already made reference to operational troops and indicated the cut which was made. Sometimes I feel that perhaps there is nothing which the department can do which is right. Last September I really thought I was doing something which everybody would applaud when the seventh and eighth divisions were disbanded. I heard nothing but criticism from one end of the country to the other. It has been talked about as a muddle; it has been said that the statement which was made was rotten. As a matter of fact, I penned the announcement myself and take full blame for it. I thought that I had made a statement which the public would understand and that we were really doing a job in cutting down operational troops. Nevertheless the storm came just the same. In spite of that, we are still studying the possibility of disbanding other units, and we are going to keep on with it regardless of what people may say and whether people give us credit for it or not.

Will the minister be able to give us now or later comparative figures of A. and T. personnel in these camps as against the number of men being trained in the camps?
Mr. RALSTON; Certainly. With regard to seeding leave I took note of what my hon. friend has said and will endeavour to see to it that early attention is given to the matter in order to ascertain whether any changes can be made which may further the objectives which he has in mind. With regard to the order in council forbidding writing to newspapers, it is not an order in council; it is Canadian army routine order, and as a matter of fact it is under consideration at this minute. With regard to the clothing allowance under general order 139-
From the tone of the minister's reply in connection with that one order or regulation may one take it that the government is taking some steps to review and perhaps alter it?
The three services are taking steps to review it.
Does that also refer to their taking part in public activities?

It was passed when I was away. I did not know the contents of it until I had it looked up here to-night. It does not refer to public activities. As I understand it, this order prohibits men writing any articles at all whether they happen to be military or otherwise. Is that what my hon. friend has reference to?
Yes.
That is the one under review by the three services now.
I hope the minister makes some change because it is pretty drastic.
Does that routine order also forbid the men writing to members of parliament?
No; Iv.R. and 0. does that.
Does that mean that any-bodj' in the armed forces cannot write to members of parliament?
On military matters.
Who is to tell?

Surely that should be
clarified. I should not like to be a party to breaking some of the K.R. and 0., but I get letters from various sources.
War Appropriation-Army
I had the sad experience in my own constituency of a constituent writing to me. I think it is a fact that K.R. and 0., as it stands now-
Surely that is pretty drastic.

I am not dealing with that because I want to get on with other matters. My hon. friend referred to general order 139. The clothing allowance provision has been made to apply to those who were discharged under general order 139, and* it has been in force since November 1.
And made retroactive.

No. With regard to soldiers' wives, my hon. friend simply referred to it as a possible activity of the department. We do want to take in all the scope possible in connection with the men who are considered the wards of the department, but I think probably that is going a little far afield. However, I shall certainly bring what my hon. friend says to the attention of the committee which has this whole matter of rehabilitation in hand. I thought my hon. friend was referring first to soldiers' brides. This is a subject which has had some attention in publications in Canada. I say in that respect that the department feels we have a responsibility there and is joining with the Department of National War Services, the Red Cross and other agencies in order to endeavour as far as possible to see to it that these girls who are coming home, some with children and some with none, are received and looked after as befits the wives of men who are fighting the battles of Canada overseas.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Weyburn said something about the breaking up of the Canadian army. I have already dealt with that. It is not a long story and it is not a very complicated one. I am not saying this sarcastically, but I never realized how the policy of having a Canadian army had taken on in Canada until the events of the last six months occurred. When the formation of the army was announced two years ago, I did not hear much applause for it anywhere. As a matter of fact, I heard a good deal of criticism in newspapers about the fact that we were aspiring to have a Canadian army. The suggestion was that we were building a structure of gingerbread, and that it was something that we were putting on to our organization by way of a frill. There was a good deal of newspaper criticism of that kind.

I find now it was regarded as a constructive step, and I am glad of that. But even a year ago I had to take notice of the criticism and to call the attention of the house to the fact that the house had approved of the organization of a Canadian army, and that I did not think it was up to the people generally, or to the house particularly, to criticize that organization which had been approved without a dissenting voice. But there was a good deal of talk-perhaps not so much in Hansard-but certainly the suggestion that we had bitten off too much, and that this idea of a Canadian army was just a little bit of frosting which could have been omitted, and that we would have been just as well off without it. The idea suggested was that it was for the purpose of making more generals, and of building up an organization which, although it did not mean much, sounded big.
That was the attitude of a good many people in Canada. But, strangely enough, just now it seems that they had real, genuine, sincere admiration and affection for that particular organization. The situation was that two years ago the Canadian army was formed. We set out to build that Canadian army, and we expected, as everybody knows, that there would have been activity on the continent of Europe at least in 1943. There was no opportunity whatsoever to give to units of the Canadian army battle experience, in view of the job which they had been given, namely the defence of Britain. The first Canadian division, then the Canadian corps and then the Canadian army itself had a key position in the defence of Britain during those years of 1940, 1941 and 1942, when the danger of invasion was imminent. That threat of invasion diminished as 1942 ran on.
The time came, in the fall of 1942, when I hoped that an opportunity might be made for the use of at least part of the Canadian army elsewhere than in Britain. I had heard a great deal of discussion and much criticism' of the fact that the Canadian army was standing idle over there. I had had some questions put to me in the House of Commons by hon. members, by members of His Majesty's loyal opposition, asking what the Canadian army was doing, and why it was not in the fighting which was then going on in North Africa.
I found out that an operation was imminent, and I immediately went to the chief of the imperial general staff with regard to the matter of possible participation of some Canadian forces in that operation. I went to the secretary of state for war. I talked the matter over thoroughly with those gentlemen, and they gave me, as I have said to the house, what I considered good and sufficient reasons why at

War Appropriation-Army
that time they could' not consider the inclusion of a Canadian component with the United States and British components of the forces which were intended to land, and which did later land in North Africa.	[DOT]
Well, the Canadian army still stayed in Britain. We still heard a good deal on this side and a good deal on the other side to the effect that the Canadian army was not doing very much. As a matter of fact, a leading Canadian in Britain at a public function on one occasion even referred to the "Canadian home guard" of the British isles. That was the attitude taken by some people. So far as I was concerned I felt we were right in respect of the attitude we had taken. I felt an opportunity would come, if some operation did not take place on the continent in the spring of 1943. If it did take place in the spring of 1943, it meant, as I said the other day, that Canada's whole investment-by that I mean an investment in lives, not dollars-of ground forces overseas would be put to the hazard in one gigantic operation across the channel, without any of them, practically, having had an opportunity of hearing a shot fired in anger. Of course, that was a situation which would have to be faced, if necessary; because, as I have said, there has to be a baptism of fire; at some time men have to hear the first shot fired. But it did seem to involve at least some responsibility, to see if it were not possible that there might be some battle experience given at least to part of the Canadian forces, if that could be done.
The opportunity came. The operation did not come off in the spring of 1943; at least the plans did not materialize. In lieu thereof there was the operation which was to take place in Sicily. An approach was made immediately to the United Kingdom authorities to suggest that there ought to be a Canadian component in the forces which were going to Sicily. Those representations were accepted, although I shall not go into detail respecting the discussions. The first Canadian division and an armoured formation were sent, and the committee knows the record made by that division and those armoured troops in Sicily and in Italy under Major-General Simmonds.
Those who talk about breaking up the Canadian army ought to think of where Canada would stand at the present time in the eyes of the world and in the eyes of her own soldiers and in the eyes of her own people, if we had not had that opportunity last July to show to the world that, notwithstanding the fact that they had not been permitted to fight for three years, Canadian soldiers were not stale,
that they could fight as did their fathers twenty-five years before them, and give a good account of themselves.
When one hears talk about breaking up the Canadian army, one asks himself: What would be the alternative? Just here let me interject that to speak of breaking up the Canadian army is not a correct description of what we are doing. We are, on the contrary, maintaining the army organization and using it as a Canadian contribution along with the corps in the United Kingdom. The alternative was, of course, to keep them all in England, to keep them all for the day when they might all launch one great attack.
I suggest to the minister another alternative: Would it not have been possible to have gone as an army?

Would my hon. friend please permit me to finish what I am saying. We felt that if we could have an opportunity to give battle training to at least a part of the army, not only the non-commissioned officers and men, but the officers themselves and the staffs, they might be available to come back to the United Kingdom-for that was to be where the main thrust was to take place. And I wish to tell the committee that for a good while nobody knew where the main thrust was going to be. As a matter of fact, it was not decided and announced until the Teheran conference. Our idea was that we would have men who would have acquired experience, and who could come back to help lead the forces who had not then had that training, in the great offensive across the channel.
That was done; the first division and an armoured formation were sent, and, as I say, a proud record for Canada was made in July and August of 1943. That involved, I suppose my hon. friend would say, the breaking up of the Canadian army, in that it involved taking one division from that army and leaving only four.
It appeared in the summer of 1943 that nobody knew what was going to happen next. There was talk, as a matter of fact, about collapse by Christmas, and that the war might be over. There was talk, on the other hand, that nobody knew when an operation might take place on the continent, and we faced the situation again of people saying, "Yes, Canada has one division out of five in the war. The other four are safely tucked away in England, and some day those four divisions will have to be thrown into battle without any battle experience." I talked the matter over with the chief of the general staff and
War Appropriation-Army

my officers at national headquarters. I talked it over with General McNaughton and I decided-I take full responsibility-upon the advice of the chief of the general staff, that for the sake of the morale of the troops in England, for the sake of the morale of the people in Canada, but much more for the sake of the training and the experience which would be obtained and which would be for the benefit of the war effort, because of the preparation we would have and the greater pool on which we could draw for the purpose of the invasion or the offensive in which we might later take part, that the thing to do was to see to it not only that non-commissioned officers and men were given an opportunity to become battle trained and battle experienced, but that our staffs, our divisional staffs and our corps staff were given an opportunity for operating in a battle theatre so that, they might know at first hand the handling, not simply in manoeuvres, but the tactical handling and administration of units and formations and divisions and corps under actual battle conditions. That was decided upon deliberately.
Representations were made again to those who had the strategic direction of the war in charge, and the result is that to-night Canada has a corps in Italy operating as a self-contained corps with just as much autonomy as the Canadian corps had under Sir Arthur Currie in 1914-18. To-night that corps is contributing many officers to the organization which is going on in the United Kingdom in order that Canada may take part in the great offensive, whenever that time may come. I shall have some announcements to make later on which will indicate that, but I cannot make them to-night. Had this action not been taken, men and senior officers would not have had this experience. The people of Canada now may know that many of the men who will lead their boys into battle will be men who have been under fire in Italy, men who have had opportunity to handle formations, men who have acted on divisional staffs under actual war conditions.
That decision was made by the Canadian government. That decision was made in respect of the Canadian army. The decision was to use the Canadian army where and how it could best be used. I say to my hon. friend that I do not for one instance make any apologies. Perhaps I am saying that a little defiantly, but I do not mean it in that way. I make that statement because of the solemn and serious responsibility which has been upon my shoulders and upon the shoulders of the government.. I wish to say earnestly and from the bottom of my heart that I believe that was 
the decision that ought to have been made. That decision was made soundly in the interests of the Canadian army and in the interests of the cause which the Canadian army is supporting.
My hon. friend asks why we did not take the whole army to Italy. The same argument applies. If you had taken them all to Italy at one time; if you had sent them all into battle at one time, you would not have had the benefit of a proportion of experienced battle-trained officers; you would not have been able to get them under war conditions by degrees. And as a matter of practice, under the situation as we found it, I do not believe there would have been any possibility of sending the whole Canadian army to Italy under the conditions which existed when the division and the corps were sent.
I believe the people of Canada would have been very much concerned if we had sent the whole Canadian force to Itah', if they were in Italy to-night, instead of the one corps that is in Italy taking its place on the right flank of the battle that is going on, with another corps in Great Britain under Canadian army headquarters. That Canadian army headquarters is in a position to direct and support and supervise any corps which our allies decide to entrust to that army. I think it is a compliment to Canadians that we are able to feel that we have an organization, that we have an army headquarters which is so organized that, when the time comes, it will be able to take on the direction and support and carry out those functions which must be exercised by an army headquarters. Under this headquarters will be a Canadian corps and whatever corps of allied troops may be associated with them. I think this is a compliment also to General McNaughton, and I say that quite frankly.
That is the story of the breaking up, so-called, of the Canadian army. I hope it will approve itself to the people of Canada. I know there will be great disappointment that all Canadians are not together. I said to this house the other day, and I emphasize and underline it to-night, that the whole course of this war, the whole fashion of formations and of battle lines to-day is in the form of task forces. There is an integration of forces of different countries. We have the special service force which has been spoken of which is made up partly of United States and partly of Canadian troops. One of the things I learned when I was in Italy was that we do not necessarily have a division fighting as a whole. We may be fighting two brigades of a division, and we may have an armoured brigade from somewhere else put along with it in order that a particular task may be done. In this

War Appropriation-Army
war Canada will be fighting side by side with the British and United States troops. There are other divisions of active armies that I know about which I cannot disclose and alongside which Canada is fighting at the present time. We cannot manage to have complete homogeneity, but at the same time we can see to it that our men are trained, that our men are fit, that our men get the best experience and are led by officers who have had experience under the actual conditions of war.
I have no doubt there will be many other questions asked in connection with this matter, but I welcome this opportunity to speak, perhaps a little at length, because I believe that when the Canadian people realize just what has happened, and why, when they know that there has been considered and deliberate judgment about this thing, they will accept the decision which has been made, believing that it is for the good of the common cause which, after all, is all that counts.

Is the increase in item 1 due solely to additional personnel, or is it due to increases in salaries and wages of men already in the service? I notice that item 2 covers officers and men, but this item 1, apparently covers civil salaries and wages.

The portion of the increase of $7,000,000 which is due to increases in pay is $552,000. This is due to the reclassification of the positions of something like 2,300 employees. The remainder is due to, first, the growth of army administration; second, the replacement of soldiers by civilians and, third, the inclusion of certain employees who previously were included under another item and who will now be deducted from that item.

It is not very often that I rise to support the government, but I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister and those who are responsible for the decision to send a Canadian division to Sicily and Italy. I know I was thrilled, and the people with whom I spoke were thrilled when they heard that Canadians were going into action as part of the eighth army, an army that had built up for itself in this war a reputation second to none. It must have been tremendously stimulating to our troops, who were green troops, to know that they were to be under the supreme command of a man who had shown that he would not start an action until he was ready, and then when he did start it. make sure that he was going places. Therefore I think we can feel gratified that our troops were sent forward under that type of leadership, and I hope that when the second mrps goes into action it will be under the same kind of leadership. Personally I would have been very uneasy if the Canadian army had gone into action as an army, with the men all green, the commanders all green and no man having proven what he could do. In a war of this kind it has been shown that with a pincers' movement it is quite easy to lose a division and even an army in a short space of time, and I congratulate the minister and his officials upon sending Canadian divisions into Sicily and Italy in the way they did.
I wish to refer for a moment to one of the matters which the minister described as one of the minor matters that had been raised.
Perhaps it was not.

I want to refer to the order which the minister said was under recom-sideration dealing with the writing of letters to the press by soldiers. I have on my desk beside me at the moment a letter from a member of the veterans' guard in which he tells me that in December he wrote a letter to the Saint John Telegraph-Journal. He is not a member of this party, but the letter dealt with some editorials and articles that were appearing in the Saint John newspaper. The letter was not published. But a week or so later, when this man was on duty one night, he was called into the orderly room and given a severe reprimand for having written a letter to this newspaper. As I say, the letter had not been published. The man thought he was entitled to express his views on matters that were of interest to him. He was a veteran of the last war with three and a half years' war service, and was discharged with wounds. He has two sons serving in the Royal Canadian Air Force in this war, one of them operating a Spitfire.
I appeal to the minister to rescind this order. After all, what are we fighting for? We are fighting for democracy, we are told. Are all the people of this country to be allowed to express themselves except the very men who are actually engaged in fighting for our right to express ourselves?
A few days ago I was reading a book written by a prominent man in Great Britain, dealing with public affairs, and in the preface to it he said that very largely the material in the book had been discussed as he was discussing it there because of the numerous political questions that had been asked him when he was addressing meetings in army camps, barracks and aerodromes in Great Britain. Only a short time ago I read an article in which it was said that one thing the British
War Appropriation-Army

were achieving in this war that our friends in the United States were not achieving was that, like Cromwell's army, the British army was becoming a thinking army, knowing exactly for what it fought, and why.
Consequently I ask the minister to consider rescinding this order. It is anti-democratic in a war of this kind when we are fighting for the principles of democracy-the right to freedom of thought, freedom of speech and freedom of association. Surely the man who is fighting for these ideals ought to be permitted to exercise some freedom in that regard. I rose to underline one of the points made by the horn, member for Weyburn and to appeal to the minister to consider doing away with this order.
' So far as writing to members of parliament is concerned, if that is covered by the king's regulations and orders, I think we should not slavishly follow K.R. and 0. of the imperial army. As my hon. friend pointed out, we have a civilian army; we represent the people of Canada in their capacity as civilians, and the men in the armed forces should, I think, have the right to write to their member and bring to his attention, not matters connected with details of military administration or anything of that sort, but matters that fall within their orbit very often, sometimes dealing with their families. May I just say, since I have been critical, that I have appreciated the manner in which the minister has himself dealt with letters of that kind having to do with matters of family need at home, and so on. Invariably the minister has given the kindliest consideration to that kind of approach, made through a member of parliament sometimes, and I wish to thank him for it. But I would suggest that he go beyond that and remove the ban on men in the armed forces writing to the press and writing to their members of parliament.

I will read the memorandum so that 'hon. members will understand that the matter is being given serious consideration:
Objections have been taken to this order on the grounds that it prohibits publication, without permission, of articles or material not of a military character. This order has recently been reconsidered by representatives of the three services.
So that the order has been reconsidered and certain recommendations are being made. I think the words "or otherwise" are the words that were objected to.

Has the Canadian army in Italy any veterinary service? I understand that the United States

army has a veterinary service which looks after meat and dairy products for the army, and meat and dairy hygiene generally. It also looks after the water supply, perishable foods and things of that sort. Has the Canadian army a similar service in Italy?

I did not see anything of the veterinary service. A member of this house, the hon. member for London, is one of the officers in charge of the Canadian Army Service Corps on the supply side. For a considerable time-this is another side of veterinary activities-mule and pack trains had to be used. But if my hon. friend is speaking of the inspection end of the veterinary service, I have not personal knowledge of it. I shall be glad to inquire and find out.
Has Canada any war dogs at the front like other armies have, the United States army, for instance?
I am not in a position to speak of that. I cannot say yes or no.
I am in the same position. I was asked the question and was not able to answer it.

Both yesterday, and time and time again to-day we have heard a lot of members suggest that many of the non-operational troops in Canada were not doing anything. I have served almost from one end of Canada to the other with operational and non-operational troops. I am, for example, at present with 1 training brigade. Some members seem to think that all that an army organization has to do to get a plethora of unnecessary people is to ask for them. Let me say that we started out with an organization in 1 training brigade that was so short of help that training cadre, cooks, clerks, officers and everybody connected with the establishment had to work Saturdays, Sundays and at nights to get the work done. I do not think I ever worked so hard in all my life before as I did on the headquarters of 1 training brigade. We were going night and day, and sometimes in a climate which is not so pleasant-Nova Scotia in the fall. Perhaps if hon. members from Nova Scotia had to be out at night in the pouring rain, they would no.t appreciate conditions around there so much as when they are inside their own houses. In any event, I can say that the attempts to get an adequate number of people to do the work which is supposed to be done, and the fight with the committee in charge, reminded me very much of the fights which I understand take place to get certain matters

War Appropriation-Army
past the treasury board. Indeed, it would seem to me harder to persuade the committee to supply an adequate staff for this work than to get authorizations from the treasury board.
I speak only of things which I know. Certainly everybody connected with the so-called non-operational group was working very hard and it was extremely difficult to persuade the committee to provide extra assistance.
That raises the question of whether people of low categories should be employed in this non-operational work. Remember that we were attempting to train young fellows, to prepare them, perhaps, to go right into action. They were young men in category "A" who had already gone through the basic, advanced and special to arms training centres. They were in the pink of condition, and the idea wTas to give them a last month of training before they might have to go into action. It was found that many of the people over age or of low category could not keep up with these young fellows-they could not train them; they could not lead them; they could not do their job adequately at times. When you suggest that none but low category people be assigned to non-operational work, you are simply proposing to train the finest men in Canada with people who are over age and of low category, and it just cannot be done.
On another matter, I was very glad that the hon. member for Acadia, a returned soldier from the last war, agreed with the government, as I believe every old soldier will agree, that no matter how much you try to train people and prepare them for actual fighting, you learn to fight only by fighting. You can learn more in regard to how to handle yourself under combat conditions by one day's experience under fire that you will probably learn in a month under similar conditions of training. I know that a real attempt has been made to simulate war conditions in the training given our troops. But, like the hon. member for Acadia, I believe that practically everybody who thought of the possibility of the whole Canadian army going into action together, without some prior experience by -arious units, was very much worried; and conversely, when it was learned that our troops vould be sent into action piecemeal, getting .heir baptism of fire without the risks which would result from the entire force being thrown in at once, with the possibility of something terrible happening to them, everybody was relieved and shared the views of the hon. member for Acadia.
In the last war the Canadian corps was built up gradually to the pitch at which it finally arrived; first a battalion, then a division, and so on; they gradually became accustomed to
the work they had to do. I do not move in exalted military circles or have the chance of consulting with the "brass hats". But, like the hon. member for Weybum, I do read a bit, and I am sure that every person who reflected seriously on the subject felt that the action which had been taken was much the wiser course, and I think the Minister of National Defence should be told that in no uncertain terms by this committee.
A word as to the question of suggesting to the troops that, every time anyone is not satisfied with something which happens to him-such as this afternoon, when we heard of somebody's complaint that he did not get his supper on time or something of that sort-he should be encouraged to write to his member of parliament or to the newspapers.
I wonder how many people who have had service in the army would expect much discipline or morale in the forces if that sort of thing were encouraged. Regular channels of communication are provided whereby a soldier i3 absolutely guaranteed that, if he has a legitimate grievance, it will be looked into. He has the right to appeal, and if he is not listened to he can take his grievance step by step to a higher authority. That means that it goes to the people who can look into it and investigate it. If he goes over the heads of those who know all about it and writes to his member of parliament, what will happen? If one person does it, the whole army is entitled to do it.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar just mentioned something of that kind. My attitude, regarding complaints made to me as a member of parliament is to say, "The law of the land has laid down full protection for you as a soldier, and you should avail yourself of the regular channels of communication. So that I as a member encourage these people to use those channels of communication. But every once in a while, someone ignores the law and writes to a member like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and gets consideration of the complaint, as he says, from the minister; and what does it lead to? The soldiers were told by members who encouraged their correspondents to abide by the laws of the land are bound to feel that they have some grievance. They see that so-and-so wrote to another member, and he went over the heads of everybody else and dealt with the minister, and got things adjusted, and they conclude that if one can do it, all can do it. What would then happen to the discipline of the army?
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggests that we should not pay much attention to what is laid down in K.R. and 0. of the

British army. I do not say we should follow it slavishly, but I suggest that the regulations contained in K.R. and 0. of the British army are there as the result of generations upon generations of experience in handling a fighting force. I also suggest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar two things: one, that no troops are better looked after by their officers or were better looked after in every way in past generations as compared with other fighting troops the -world over than British troops; second, that because of, or perhaps the hon. member may say, in spite of these conditions in the past from time to time in various wars there was built up, in the British army, a body of fighting men not excelled by any equivalent force of fighting men anywhere else in the world. The history of what they have done on various battle fields for the last several hundred years is enough to establish that.
