Coming back to the matter I was discussing, I agree it might be possible to consider these regulations in the light of changed conditions and that this should be done; but having had something to do with the army in the last war as a private, and something to do with the army in this war, I fMr. Tucker.]
would say that the first place that a soldier Should be encouraged to go if he has any difficulties at all is to the officer who is in immediate charge of him, who is told over and over again that his duty is to encourage his men to come to him with their most intimate problems; and who should feel that it is his duty to convince his men that they can come to him and confide in him. There should be a feeling of real comradeship. If the man feels he is not getting a square deal from the officer immediately in charge of him, he has the right to go to the officer who is next higher in rank; and if he is still not satisfied1 that he is receiving fair treatment, it is his right to go higher and higher and higher. But by making it necessary for that soldier to go in the first instance to the officer, the officer will probably be able to clear up the difficulty there and then. There is, however, something more important than that. If the soldier is taught to use, and if he tries to use that means of obtaining redress, he will find nine times out of ten that the difficulty under which he is suffering will be cleared up by his own officer. This would lead to greater mutual confidence and it would enable them to learn to get together and to trust one another. But if you encourage every soldier to believe that if he has some sort of grievance against his officer he can write to his member of parliament, and the member of parliament can go after the officer commanding that battalion and get that officer into' trouble, w'hat sort of army will you have very shortly?
There is another matter that I would call to the minister's attention, and I think he will agree that it is most important. I understand that in the beginnidg applications for farm leave and postponement of service were sent by the district officers commanding to national defence headquarters and were then referred back to the national selective boards. That meant presumably that troops, no matter from what part of Canada they came, received the same consideration. The decision has now been made, embodied in a routine order, that applications for farm leave shall be dealt with by district officers commanding. That may have been necessary at a time when there was, for example, real danger of attack on the Pacific coast, leaving it to the district officer commanding there, or the G.O.C., Pacific command, to say whether the exigencies of the service would permit him to allow anyone to go on farming leave or to have postponement of service by reason of the fact that he was needed at home on the farm. But the effect of that has been this. There were, I understand, somewhere in the neighbourhood of
6,000	people who were granted extended leave.

War Appropriation-Army
If so, it would appear to me that there has been a good deal more generosity in the granting of such leave in other places than to men in the troops in the Pacific command. I do not think there is any doubt about it. That may have been justified when the exigencies of the service were different from what they are to-day; but I would urge the minister to see to it that applications for postponement, or for seeding leave, or harvest leave, or leave on compassionate grounds, be dealt with in some uniform manner throughout Canada, so that it would not be possible for one D.O.C. to turn down all applications almost en masse, while another D.O.C., who is more favourably inclined to or more impressed with the needs of the farming industry, grants far more applications than are granted elsewhere.
I do not know the figures; but if there has been granted the number that the minister says, then my experience leads me to say that if other constituencies had the same experience in getting farm leave granted, the number would not be 6,000 but more like
1,000.	That is probably due to the fact that such a large proportion of troops called up from my constituency and in Saskatchewan have been serving in the Pacific command.
I do not ask for special consideration. I simply suggest that the same attitude be taken toward the troops everywhere, no matter where they may be in Canada, and that there should be some supervision over the decisions of the district officers commanding. That is possible now because the danger of invasion and the exigencies of the service are such that perhaps conditions are pretty much the same throughout Canada.
I did not catch the suggestion as to who the supervising authority should be. Did the hon. member mean that it should come back to headquarters?
I think it is better that it should come back to headquarters in Ottawa and they can see that similar treatment is given to the people in all military districts.

I rather think that if the members of the house generally are labouring under the impression that a large number of those in the forces are desirous of writing directly to members of parliament, they might be shocked in some instances to know the reaction of large numbers of the forces to that somewhat unique animal the member of parliament-in-general. Individually, I suppose, the average member is as well regarded by those persons whom he knows in the forces as any other member of society; but as a group, it is very revealing and produces a good deal of thought to sit by, and I wall not 100-34i
say in disguise but at least unknown, and listen sometimes to the comments which one hears with respect to the activities of those of us who occupy seats in this house.
I should say at once that I welcome the suggestion of the minister to-night that the objectionable words in the regulations quoted, with respect to the publishing of letters sent home and to private individuals by persons in the forces, are likely to be altered, because under the strict conditions of censorship which now exist, it suggests rather too much that the forces themselves are not sufficiently security-minded and not sufficiently patriotically-minded to be able to exercise that type of discretion which would make it possible for the letter which is written to the home town to receive that degree of publicity which the family of the man or the man himself might welcome.
This brings me to another consideration which I think is of importance, and that is the general method or lack of method in keeping the personnel serving in the active forces informed as to what is going on at home, and particularly with respect to Canada's war effort as a whole and in some degree of things political. I am not one of those persons who ever felt, even in times of peace, that there was either sense or justification in the virtual disenfranchisement of those persons who served in the active forces, and if I was not sympathetic with it in times of peace, I am even less sympathetic in time of war.
I am. not aware that soldiers of modern nations in this war such as Russia fight any less well because they are active members of a political organization.-I said a political organization in that particular case, but I think it would apply where there is more choice. I do not think soldiers fight any better for a society which they hope will come in some nebulous time in the future than they will fight for a state of society which they help to create and in which they have a vital interest.
As I went among the overseas forces in the United Kingdom in the last few months I had an opportunity of sitting in at a considerable number of discussion groups. The discussion groups to which I refer that are held in the Canadian army are known as leaderless-situa-tion groups. Half a dozen men are put in a room and examined by people trained to make such examinations, in order to see which one of these groups under certain circumstances will assert himself as a natural leader, and which of the men will fail to measure up to these tests. One of the tests frequently used, not only in our army but in other armies, is that of the leaderless-diseussion group. A half
524	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Army
dozen men. would be put in a room for about thirty-five minutes and told that they could talk about anything they liked, but that they must express opinions on the subject chosen. They are told also that they are being observed. If they were not observed they would not be there.
If I can trust my memory I attended twelve or thirteen such groups. Those groups were composed of young chaps who had been overseas anywhere from two and a half to four years. Without exception one of the subjects which was nominated by someone was the question of reestablishment and rehabilitation after the war. That subject was not always discussed. They get very much interested in subjects like whether we can defeat the hun by air power without an attack on the continent. There were a variety of subjects, but I want to point out that that particular one was always mentioned and very often discussed.
If I may say so, I was shocked to hear these men talking about the days after the war in the exact terms of the days before the war which we remember rather sadly. I sometimes had an opportunity to hear some extreme statement from these boys. They would urge that we must attempt to do something which I knew that the people of Canada have already done, perhaps two or three years ago, for example, in connection with the expansion of industry. I would ask the question, "Do you know So-and-so", and they would almost invariably say, "no". I might then give them a word of explanation, perhaps in the discussion period, and they would say, "You have been in Canada recently; what about this and that?" Their curiosity was insatiable. Their interests tended always to the future days rather than to what had gone before. I found very little recrimination among any of the boys against society as a whole, for the experience through which many of them had gone. I found an appalling lack of knowledge of what was going on. And when I drew attention to that they would say. "Why don't they send somebody over .to tell us?" Well, you know in a democracy who "they" are. There is only one "they" who can do anything under a democratic governmental system.
When discussions were over somebody would say, "Don't you think there is something in it. Someone should be sent to tell them." I would answer, "Canada has only been able to do what she has done by virtue of the fact that every man and woman in the country has supported the authorities there." It is not the government that has done the job, but the

Canadian people; the direction and executive part of it has been done by the government, but if we are going to tell the story of what has been done w7e must tell the story of what has been accomplished by the executive action of the government. Suppose some one was sent to tell that story. Suppose, even that, some of my hon. friends to the left or I should attempt to write that story to these men. The cry would go up from different sections of this country that the Canadian army was developing a system of political commissars with all its implications. Therefore I do say that it is perhaps impractical to do that. However, I think every possible means should be taken to put the story before thesq boys. A large percentage of them have no real assurance of coming back. The war has scarcely started for them. In spite of that they are thinking in terms of the future, and to those who come back and to their children it is of vital interest. They should have the information; they should be encouraged to discuss it, to think about it and to talk about it. That is a little different from saying they should be encouraged to write to the newspapers or members of parliament about personal and individual grievances. I know something of the problems of discipline in the army. I have had some opportunities to study some of the disciplinary actions in the army and at a later date I shall probably have something to say about that.
We ought to cultivate the idea of getting to these men, somehow, more of the details of the nation's affairs. These men have a bigger stake in the future of this country than any of us. We cannot get this information out to them by radio because the majority of them who are situated in England have no access to it. We are not getting it to them, unfortunately, to the extent that they desire, in the way of pamphlets or general information. It is important to the morale of the army in much the same way as is the mail which was referred to by the minister and the leader of the opposition. I do not need to stress that because enough has been said about it.
Are they getting a good supply of newspapers over there?

Newspapers do not go across. The trouble with newspapers is that by the time they reach them they are so old and remote from the troop's knowledge and experience that they are scarcely news. I saw this experiment made:	papers of Ottawa and
Montreal were laid on the table in an officers' mess within thirty hours of the time they came from the presses. They were placed in a conspicuous pile. One young man who had been over there for two or three years came

War Appropriation-Army
in and glanced at them. His face lit up. It was something from home. He looked at them, sort of glanced through them casually and then went over and read the British paper which he was accustomed to reading, because there was nothing in his recent experience and understanding that attracted him to the Canadian papers. The headlines did not relate to anything in his daily experience. Four years is a long time, and unfortunately for us in this house and, to a certain degree the people of Canada as a whole, too much of the information that reaches the men about what is going on here is of the sensational type and, I am sorry to say, not always in a reliable form. You cannot be surprised if they write and request news and information, if they wish to be informed on current opinion. We should not be surprised if they feel the responsibility of citizenship in this country. We should be glad. I have come back with it firmly fixed in my mind that everything should be done to make these men and women feel that they are fully enfranchised citizens of Canada. I am firmly of the opinion that they must have a full understanding of what is going on at home.
Before I sit down I should like to mention one more experience I had. Not very long ago I sat in the mess of a bomber command. A visitor in the mess was a chap who had just come back from the near east. I never heard a man get a better hearing than he received when he bragged, frankly, bragged, a Canadian among Canadians, about what it felt like as a Canadian to land in a port in the near east, or at a station somewhere in Africa and walk up from the landing-strip, or from the docks, between crates piled on either side like an avenue on which were letters four or five inches high saying, "made in Canada". That sort of thing got a reaction which would be soul-warming to those people who produced the goods that were there. The discussions with respect to those people who sometimes through mistaken or selfish ideas have stopped for a while producing these goods, would be shocking if heard.

I wish to say a brief word on this item. I listened carefully to the minister when he made his first statement yesterday and I have also listened to him to-day. The more we listen, the more information we get. I think the minister made a frank and proper statement in reply to the hon. member for Weyburn. It was informative, and I believe it would have been well if he had made it a little earlier rather than have it prompted by the hon. member. I certainly appreciate, and I think we all do, the difficulty the minister and the government have in carrying on the
war. The minister has the first responsibility. He has to organize the Canadian army and keep it supplied with reinforcements, the stream-line training he speaks about. That has to be ready and he does not know the minute he will be called on. I think it was very fine that he set out in an instructive way to give us the information which he did. We have heard a good deal with respect to soldiers, or other men in the armed forces writing to members of the House of Commons, or taking their difficulties to district officers commanding. The minister has said that teamwork is necessary, and I think hon. members ought to be patriotic enough to display a desire for teamwork.
May I tell the committee how I have dealt with many of these men who have come to me-and I have no doubt other hon. members are approached in the same way. All of us receive many letters. I have three on my desk which came yesterday. I have not yet received my western mail for to-day because the train is late, but I suppose there will be more when that mail arrives. To be quite frank, I reply to these men or, if they come to my office-and a great many of them have come-I listen to their stories. Some of them think they have grievances. I say to them, "Well, you may have a grievance", if I think they have one. I tell them how to go about obtaining redress, and point out to them that the first thing for them to do is to discuss the matter with their district officer commanding.
That is what I tell them because, as I have said on many occasions, if the Minister of National Defence were to listen to me or to any other member of parliament, would not this whole thing be a farce? There have to be rules and regulations, and the minister is familiar with them. It is the duty of hon. members to tell these men just how to go about obtaining redress for their grievances. While I have had cases brought to my attention where I did not believe they had received a square deal after the matter had been taken up with the district officer commanding, yet on the other hand I believe many of them have received just treatment.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that some action will be taken with respect to having men return on leave to take part in seeding operations. This afternoon we heard a long discussion in connection with the forestry corps, some of whom were turned over to do farming operations. I make an appeal to the minister to have the information sent out in plenty of time so that the farmers will receive a square deal in getting assistance from some of the non-operational troops we now have in Canada.
War Appropriation-Army

I could go into detail by pointing out that in my opinion some of the boys overseas, who have been there for three or four years, should be returned to Canada. In some instances fathers may have died, or something of that kind happened, and where fathers have died widows would be left on farms. In those circumstances it is, of course, difficult to carry on.
I make a further appeal to the minister. Yesterday he said he proposed to enlist 60,000 men this year. I trust, when that is done, the call-up wall be carried on in a manner which will not bring about the discrimination and unfairness which obtained in respect of the call-up made last year. At page 190 of Hansard are to be found figures showing the call-up in the thirteen military districts. My observations apply more particularly to the western provinces. We find according to those figures that in a western district with only ane-third of the population of districts in certain parts of eastern Canada the percentage at Regina was 8, whereas in the east it was only 5-7. Those are percentages taken for 100 troops called up.
Possibly the minister will recall the statement made by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and he might follow the suggestions made by that hon. member. When this year's call-up is made I wish to see a fair and equitable call in all military districts. I make that appeal to the minister, and trust he will take into consideration what I have said.

On the last point, I do not wish to pass the buck, but I must say that those call-ups are made by means of requisitions on the Minister of Labour by the Department of National Defence. It is the Department of Labour and national selective service which actually carry on the call-up in any particular district. So that I am afraid all the army can do is to ask for so many men to report at a certain centre at a certain time- and that might be at Vancouver, or anywhere else. National selective service calls them up from any part of Canada. We do not regulate where they are to come from. We only specify where we went them to report. However, I ^hail pass on to the Minister of Labour what my hon. friend has said. There is nothing I can do further than that.
I have already made a statement with respect to seeding leave. That will be taken into consideration almost at once, and I think the farmers, who were getting a pretty square deal from the army-and I hope my hon. friend does not think they are not-will be treated fairly-[DOT]

I did not say that.
(Mr. Perley.]
-particularly having regard to the fact that there is very liberal, shall I say-if my hon.. friend does not mind that term-
Progressive, probably.

-a very liberal exemption or deferment for men who are engaged in farming. However, the point has been raised to-night, and I shall endeavour to look into it and give it the best possible consideration.
I am obliged to the hon. member for Rosthern, the hon. member for Winnipeg South and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for their remarks respecting representations made to members of parliament. As I said to the leader of the opposition a little while ago, I wish to call to the attention of the committee a paragraph in K. R. and O. to which I believe some hon. members have been referring. I would point out that the provision is not against the writing of letters to members of parliament. I refer to section 423 (b) which states that attempts to obtain favourable consideration of any application by the use of outside influence are forbidden, and, if resorted to, will be regarded as an-admission on the part of the applicant that the case is not good on its merits, and that it will be dealt with accordingly. That is the section under which men, offend if they write to members of parliament, or others outside the service, if thereby they seek, in the words of the regulation "to obtain favourable consideration", a promotion, a transfer, or something of that kind.
I have had experience in my own constituency; do not let hon. members think I do not understand this matter. I appeal to members of parliament to have these young men realize that this thing called "pull"-and that is what they call it-does not exist. As. sure as the world, when you find a young man who goes to a member <?f parliament, or writes to the minister, and as a result thereof some favourable consideration ensues, just as sure as the world he tells someone else the result, and the story goes that Bill has got something by way of "pull." It does not matter how regular the procedure may have been. The suggestion arises because the action was taken by a member of parliament or someone outside the service.
I have, received representations from time to time from members and I do endeavour to deal with them. I do not for a moment question the right of hon. members to write me with respect to these young men, but I do believe the teamwork mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle could help us all so that these young men might not be encouraged to write to members of parliament

War Appropriation-Army
respecting matters having to do with their positions in the army-and particularly those communications dealing with promotions or for special consideration of some sort.
I say in that connection-and this is almost a humiliating confession

that we almost have to apologize to Canadian military headquarters in England when we make an inquiry about any individual, for fear someone will think that influence is being used within the meaning of section 423(b). I know that should not be so; but the less there is of that sort of thing, the easier it will be to run the army. It would mean that everyone would feel they were being dealt with on exactly the same basis.
I had an instance-a very sorry one-in my own experience, in which I was written to by an individual. I did not see the letter. It was passed to the branch concerned. Next thing I found out was that the man had forfeited fourteen days' pay for having written to his member of parliament. That was serious for him, particularly in view of the fact that his member of parliament happened to be the Minister of National Defence. He is still out the fourteen days' pay. He said he thought he was writing to the Minister of National Defence-and so he was; but the letter got into a groove, and reached someone who was pretty tough on the regulations, with the result that a forfeiture of pay was imposed. I think it would do us all good; I think it would do the army good if we endeavoured to teach the provisions of this section 423(b) to the soldiers in our constituencies. We should ask them, not to not write to us, but not to write to ask for favourable consideration in connection with army matters, not to make representations outside.
As the hon. member for Rosthern says, there is a plain line of procedure laid down. It is pretty old, but it is pretty sound. It promotes confidence between the man and his officer, and puts the officer in the position of being a trustee and a guardian for the man. He is his adviser and friend. Generally a man's complaint is considered and he gets satisfaction. I know that sometimes a man must be persistent. He may have a platoon officer who is not very sympathetic and he may have to go to his company officer, but in the end he gets through and the grievance is redressed.

I wish to support what the hon. member for Winnipeg South has said about getting information to the men in our armed forces. I understand there is a department known as the department of public relations. I should like a statement from the
minister about what is being done and whether every use possible is being made of this department to get information to the armed forces in the different fields. The longer this war lasts, the more important this will be.
Another matter I wished to take up concerns increases in pay. An increase was announced last year, but this was contingent upon the officer commanding making a recommendation. I understand in some cases the increase was ten cents a day after three months' service, and in other cases after six months' service. I should like to have an assurance from the minister that this increase is now in general effect throughout the service, both in the army and the N.R.M.A. forces.
In connection with writing to members of parliament my experience has been that the men who write to me are ignorant of the machinery which they could use to approach their officers. The hon. member for Rosthern has said that the men are told what to do, but I have found that many of them do not know what to do. They thought they were supposed to go to the sergeant-major or the sergeant, and they got told in sergeant-major language what they can'do with their letters. It seems to me that in many of the camps there has not been sufficient instruction given to the men and they are entirely at a loss to know what the procedure is. If the men were given more instructions; if they knew what their rights and privileges were and that there would be redress for a particular situation, then when letters come to members of parliament they could advise the men to take up their case in the proper way. I tell men who write to me that if they cannot get access to the officials in that way I shall be glad to take up the matter. I find that in most cases when they try the proper procedure they get fairly quick action.
I should like to support what has been said this evening with regard to compassionate leave. There seems to be considerable difference in the action taken by various commands in connection with men applying for leave on compassionate grounds, or for spring and harvest leave. I would support any move that might be made to make this procedure more uniform, either by having these applications go through headquarters or by giving definite instructions to the units with regard to the action that should be taken.
Several demands have been made in this house-I made one myself in 1940-for free transportation for our soldiers when on leave or furlough. Surely these men and women who are offering everything should be granted free transportation on our railroads.
War Appropriation-Army

Would you apply that to
N.R.M.A.?
Embarkation leave.

You referred to the men
and women who were offering everything and I was wondering if you would include them both.

The N.R.M.A. men
are to be sent overseas if they are required. Canada is a country of great distances and some of these men are being discriminated against. It seems to me that the least we can do for these people is to grant them free transportation. Thousands of our men have been lost in the last year, and I hate to think that some of them were denied the privilege of seeing their loved ones before they went overseas because the cost of transportation was too great. The minister stated this afternoon that the matter was under consideration, but it has been under consideration for over a year. Nothing has been done about it. Some reduction was made in. 1941, but I think we should go a little further. It may be said that we should not encourage increased travel in these days, but I am sure the civilian population would be ready to step aside if necessary so that these men might go home on their last leave or furlough.
The last thing I wish to refer to is something disgraceful that occurred* recently in a Montreal court. Last week a discharged soldier was sent to gaol for two months for wearing a uniform illegally. No doubt he was wearing the uniform illegally because he had been discharged two weeks previously. When this particular soldier was demobilized the winter clothing allowance was only $35, but I understand it has been raised to $65. When a man is discharged in Canada in the winter time $35 is not sufficient to buy his civilian outfit. Surely such a thing should not happen in this land of ours. The regulations should be changed so that this thing cannot occur again. I understand that some action is being taken. The Minister of Justice Should be notified of this and if the sentence cannot be remitted, I think some other action should be taken so that the men in our fighting forces will know that such a thing cannot 'happen again.

Did the hon. member
bring that to our attention before?

No. There was an
editorial in the Montreal Star of February 5. I have not the name of the soldier.
That is only a report by a newspaper. The hon. member should read the judgment and the circumstances.
I read the judgment.

A short time ago the minister stated that his department would requisition the number of men required in each district from the selective service. I should like to know upon what the requisition is based. Does it take into consideration the number of voluntary enlistments in the military district, or is dt based upon the population in the district? What is the basis of these requisitions? It seems to me that requisitions are made against certain districts where there has been a large voluntary enlistment. They naturally feel that they must fill the requisition. I think there should be a different basis for making the requisitions from the various military districts.
I wish to say something about agricultural leave. Last year, as I understand it, the person who made application for agricultural leave applied to the officer commanding. In many cases the officer commanding flatly refused to consider the application and it never reached the district officer commanding. I agree with the hon. member for Rosthem that a different method should be used this year to bring about more uniform procedure in the granting of agricultural leave. I had several cases brought to my notice last year of men being granted agricultural leave to work on a farm where there were only thirty to forty acres under cultivation, while in other cases applications were refused when the men wanted agricultural leave to work on farms where their fathers had a section or a section and a half under cultivation; yet they received no consideration. I would urge again that a more uniform method be used in the granting of agricultural leave whereby the needs of each particular case might be given consideration.

With regard to the requisitions, I want the committee to understand that all that the Department of National Defence does in the matter is to say that we want so many men at a certain training centre. The national selective service directorate decide where to get these men. They may not get them from that particular district at all. The Department of National Defence has nothing to do with designating the district from which the men shall be drawn. It simply says: We want so many men at a certain training centre.
With regard to having a more uniform system for considering applications for agricultural leave, I have the point made by the hon. member for Rosthern and the hon. member for Melfort, and I will look into that and have it brought before the officers who will be dealing with the matter very shortly.
The hon. member for Yorkton asked in regard to increased pay, and I might as well put that on the record now. He asked as to

War Appropriation-Army
the percentage of men overseas and in Canada who are receiving the increased rates of pay provided under the order of last year. The survey is not complete, but it gives a fair cross-section which enables us to tell pretty well what the whole situation is.
Overseas, the number in receipt of the basic rate of SI.50 is 90-5 per cent; the number in receipt of SI.40 is 4-5 per cent; the number in receipt of $1.30 is 5 per cent. In the C.W.A.C. the number in receipt of $1.25 is 50 per cent; the number in receipt of $1.10 is 7-1 per cent; the number in receipt of $1.05 is 42-9 per cent. To get this C.W .A.C. figure, for the purpose of getting these results they took about half the personnel over there. It may not be quite an accurate cross-section, but it would be pretty nearly so.
Why are the women not paid on an equal footing with the men in the army?

As I have explained before, a quick answer would be that it is not the practice in connection with other women's corps. It is the same with the ATS and the Wrens. The theory rvas, in plain English, that women were not adaptable to all forms of service. While they did exceedingly well the jobs that they could do, they were not as versatile, if I may put it in that way, as the men, having regard to the different forms of heavy service that the men have to do. That is the only answer I know. I have made the same answer to the hon. member for North Battleford and to the hon. member for Edmonton East.
Is there any difference between the pay of the Wrens, the women's division of the air force and the C.W A.C. for equal ranks?

No, none; they are on an even basis. My hon. friend will remember that they were all increased last year. They were receiving 663 per cent of the men's pay and that was increased to 80 per cent. Tradeswomen get the same trades pay as the tradesmen.

Has the government
under consideration raising the pay of the women generally to that of the men?
No. Their basic pay is 80 per cent of a man's pay.
I hope that answer is a little more elastic than it sounds.
Things are always under consideration, I suppose.
There is active and passive consideration, and quite a difference between them.

In Canada the number in receipt of the basic rate of $1.50 is 65-7 per cent; the number in receipt of $1.40, 9-1 per cent; the number in receipt of $1.30, 25-2 per cent.
In Canada the women's army corps has 60-1 per cent in receipt of $1.20; 11*5 per cent in receipt of $1.10; and 28-4 per cent in receipt of $1.05.
There seems to be quite a difference in the pay of the C.W .A.C. overseas and those in Canada. There is a larger percentage on the lower rate of pay overseas. Is there any explanation for that?

Overseas 50 per cent were in receipt of the top rate, as compared with 60 per cent in Canada. Perhaps it was because there were more tradeswomen in Canada. But when I think of it, that, of course, does not apply with regard to the basic rate. I cannot give the explanation of that offhand, but I shall make inquiries.
Do the C.WA.C. get a clothing allowance?
They get a cash allowance for clothing.
Have their uniforms to last for the duration of the war?
No; the uniform lasts as long as it lasts. When the inspecting officer decides that it is no longer serviceable, they get another.
Does the government give them another uniform when that is warranted?
Yes.
You should not ask ladies to put up with a uniform until it is worn out.
Oh, no, I do not say that.
Has any consideration been given to granting an allowance in respect of girls with dependent mothers?

On July 1, 1943, provision was put into effect bringing dependent mothers within the meaning of dependents under the regulations.
The hon. member for Yorkton asked in regard to the steps taken to get the news to the troops. The Canadian Press bulletin, as the committee knows, is cabled overseas to Canadian troops. It is published twice a
War Appropriation-Army

week; I am not sure but that it is oftener than that. It has a very wide circulation among all three services, particularly the army, because they are more concentrated. The air force find it more difficult to get it when they are serving with R.A.F. squadrons. The bulletin is greatly appreciated by the troops and has done a genuine service.
How many copies are printed?
I think probably there is one copy for every four or five men.
Is it printed overseas? Mr. RALSTON: Yes.
The news is assembled here and sent overseas?
Yes.
Would it be possible to have a copy of the news which is sent overseas circulated to the members of this house, in order that we may see what it contains?

I will try to do better still. My hon. friend has put the idea in my mind. We can get a few copies of the bulletins sent over in a bomber. I should like hon. members to see the bulletin. I take a little credit for this Canadian Press bulletin. I was over in 1940 and I was shocked and ashamed to be asked in November by some of our boys who were guarding an aerodrome, "Who won the world series?" I decided that if the Canadian troops were that badly informed, we had better get a newspaper and get it quickly.
They did not ask who had won the election in 1940?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Who did win the world
series?
It was in 1940.
Did the minister know who won the world series?

I could tell them then, yes. Hon. members may be interested in a publication which has been going for some months overseas, "Canadian Affairs", which seems to have been of considerable interest to the troops. It is published under the auspices of the wartime information. Perhaps members of the committee have seen it. The second issue of the home edition is just out. It deals with articles which perhaps are more for study groups, as has been suggested, but it has a good deal of factual information as well.
Is any arrangement being made for that pamphlet, "Canadian Affairs," to be distributed to the troops overseas in the same fashion as the news sheet is?
As the Canadian Press bulletin is?
Yes, in the same generous measure.
I am assuming that it will be.
As a matter of fact, at the moment it is not.
As a matter of fact, the distribution so far has been mostly to officers, has it not?
Yes, to officers, by whom the reading is casual; but every copy that gets to the troops is "read to pieces", because in it they get some elements of opinion as well as news.

I am glad to get that testimonial to it, and consideration will be given to sending it out on a larger scale. As a matter of fact, we have only just commenced using it in Canada. The first issue of the home edition, dated January 15, is in my hands now.
In Italy the only really Canadian paper . there was the Red Patch, a little paper published in Naples. It was gotten out by the first division and was most creditable as a purely house organ. In addition to that they had the Eighth Army News. It had a small box section for Canadian news, but that was pretty small. There has now been established the Maple Leaf, and the first copy was issued on January 14. It is published at Naples and is serviced by Canadian Press with home news; it will also be a house organ; that is, it will have some news of the units at the same time. It is more along the lines of the United States Stars and Stripes, which is published for the American army.
I think that answers the question as to the way in which news is being gotten to the troops. In addition, broadcasts are being made from England from time to time, but often these are not heard by the troops unless they are out of the line, whereas the Maple Leaf and the Red Patch get up the line to the troops, and are eagerly read. I found in North Africa, when I was in the reinforcement camps, a great shortage of reading matter in the form of magazines like the Reader's Digest and other like and light literature. Everything hon. members can do to assist in getting more of that sort of thing to the troops will be, I am sure, of genuine assistance to morale.
My hon. friend mentioned the matter of fares. I have nothing more to say about that, but it has been under consideration. The consideration which was given reduced the cost to the soldier to one-third of a single fare for

War Appropriate-Army
a return journey, and that was regarded as a pretty substantial measure of assistance to the troops. Take, for example, Camp Borden to Vancouver; the return coach fare is $87.55; the soldier obtains return accommodation for $15.95. Then from Halifax to Vancouver the ordinary return fare is $131; for the soldier it is $25.10. The same transportation concession as is allowed when proceeding on annual leave and furlough is granted when the individual is given embarkation leave. The only phase of the matter I mentioned this afternoon that we had under further consideration was the possibility that the ceiling of the contribution a soldier makes might be fixed at some definite amount. We have that under consideration now and under discussion with the railway companies.
I have made a note of the case of which my hon. friend spoke, of a man in Montreal who had been wearing a uniform illegally, and will inquire into it at once.

Regarding the point
which the minister has just brought up, concerning lower fares for soldiers on furlough or otherwise, a good many of us through the years have attempted to persuade the government to grant free transportation under certain circumstances to the troops. The government has, of course, conceded something on this point, and we are always glad to acknowledge any movement in that direction. There may be reasons, although I have never been convinced they are very good, why free transportation should not be given to the troops at all times, but I think the minister might, even at this late date, reconsider the provision of free transportation on the railways on the six months' furlough and the embarkation leave. I reiterate this appeal because there is a feeling abroad that some of the little things which do not cost the country very much, but mean so much to the troops in Canada before they leave, are not being taken care of. Sometimes we are penny-wise and, perhaps, pound-foolish. It would be well to disregard the little extra money it would take and make this gesture, even though it be nothing more than a gesture, to the troops in Canada before they leave. It would show that our government and our people are making a move in recognition of the sacrifices which these young men are prepared to make on behalf of all of us.
Then there is a feeling, to which I have heard expression given, as no doubt the minister has on many occasions, that the armed forces of our friends to the south are being serviced by the government and the people of the United States on what is sometimes regarded as a higher standard than our own. I do not wish to make any comparisons or cast any reflections on the manner in which our
own troops are being used, but I suggest that Canada cannot afford to use her troops, while they are here or on the scene of actual operations in accordance with any lower standard than that of any other country. It may be that my information on these points is wrong, but I have heard it voiced by the troops themselves, and that is why I put it before the minister. Last evening I brought up a matter which, though perhaps not of large importance, was sufficiently so for the minister to mention it, and seemed to me sufficiently important to emphasize, namely, that the public should see to it that our people overseas get plenty of mail and are kept in frequent contact with the community in which they lived.
My hon. friend is quite right; it is not a little thing.

To some people it may seem a small thing, but it is of tremendous importance; and so are such matters as transportation. These are things that may not mean in the aggregate a great deal of money, but I think they would pay great dividends in the future from the point of view of our forces. The minister is in a better position than I am to know that the troops look at these little things as an evidence of what the government thinks of their services and of the appreciation of the country. It shows how the country recognizes the sacrifices they are prepared to make, and I feel keenly in the matter. With the expenditure of a little more money a great deal could be done to enhance the prestige of our people at home, and also of the government, with our troops. We should see to it that all these little differences that sometimes naturally crop up in the minds of the troops are eradicated. As you ride on *the trains and talk to the troops you get to know what they are thinking. You do not have to raise the question; it is brought up time and again.
Some years ago I raised the question, as I have done on many other occasions, with reference to free transportation. Dozens of soldiers on the trains find out who you are *and they say that this is something that should be taken into consideration. It is something that has caught on with the troops. They have never been able to see why, when we are able to spend so much money on so many things, some little conveniences of this sort are not provided for them. I concur in this idea and I should like to see Canada stand high at home with the troops overseas. I am not suggesting that this is not the case, but there are many little things that we could have done and can still do to improve our position at home, and the esteem in which we
War Appropriation-Army

are held by our fighting men. I am sure the minister will be sympathetic, but I should like him to give the matter more than passive consideration, because frankly, in view of the fact that the United States has the reputation of doing these things in a big way, I think we in Canada must measure up to the standard set by other countries. In fact, I should like to see this country do a little better than the rest.
As a matter of fact, in this regard the United States is behind us. They charge full fare.
I was not thinking of railway transportation particularly, but of servicing overseas.

I should have said they charge three-quarters fare. My hon. friend is quite right. There are some things which the United States certainly does in a big way; but without casting any reflection upon them, or preening ourselves on being a little more modest in our appropriations, I would suggest that there are directions in which I do not think I would go as far as the United States- for instance, provision with regard to hostels and things of that kind. They are extremely comfortable, but we have got along with less of that sort of -thing, and have got along very well indeed. I do not take second place to anyone, not even to my hon-. friend, in the desire to see 'the best possible done for the troops, consistent with this idea, that we want them to realize that this is a war and this is a war service we are providing, that these things are temporary, and that soldiers as well as civilians do help the country not only by fighting but by saving, provided reasonable comfort is obtained.
In the matter of fares, I feel that we have gone a long distance, having regard to what the United States has done; of course in Britain, there are free fares as in the last war. Our system in Canada is a so-rt of half-way house that would seem to be reasonable,. I have heard what my hon. friend has -had to say and have heard- similar representations before, and these matters are always under consideration.

The minister referred to mothers' allowances paid in respect of persons serving overseas. I should like to have a little more information in regard to mothers' allowances paid to mothers of men in the armed forces abroad. As I understand it, a mother whose son is serving overseas cannot receive mother's allowance unless the father is totally incapacitated. That

places the family in an extremely bad position. I am thinking of a particular case. The father of this family is a janitor who is receiving a very small amount for his services in a schooL house. The mother has applied for mother's allowance. In this case there is a portion of assigned pay, but I am informed that the regulation is such that no mother's allowance can be given unless the father is totally incapacitated from earning a livelihood. If that is true, that is a terrible position for these people to be placed in. Is it understood that assigned pay in a case such as I have indicated is to be used by the mother as a means of livelihood? I understand that the assigned pay is not necessarily used for that purpose. If it is, however, then certainly the government cannot expect that soldier will have saved up for him two or three or four hundred dollars to enable him to take up a farm when he comes home under the arrangements now proposed. Will the minister give some information along that line?

I believe the hon. member is dealing with the case of a soldier's mother whose husband is alive but is totally incapacitated from earning a living. Is he criticizing the provision with regard to total incapacitation, or has he in mind that it must be shown that the soldier is not her sole support?
Not necessarily her sole support. I believe the regulation reads that before the mother can receive mother's allowance the father must be totally incapacitated from earning a living.

That is correct. It is
section 101. What my hon. friend is asking is that the regulation be changed?

Yes, definitely so, because the father may be earning a small amount, $5 a month, and yet the mother is barred entirely from, receiving mother's allowance and that might be her only source of income. I have such a case in mind and that is why I mentioned it.

The section is a familiar one. The same thing appears in the Pension Act, where there is a requirement to show that the husband is totally incapacitated, but I cannot speak to it with any degree of certainty to-night. I will take it under consideration and consult the dependents' allowance board.
What about a deserted mother? I fancy that was altered.

The mother whose husband has deserted her and who has not -been supporting her for a considerable length of

Supply-Agriculture
time, where the officer or soldier is her sole or partial support? That is taken care of. Because she is deserted she is not getting any support at all.
Would the minister explain the point I brought up in connection with that. Is it expected that the mother would use the assigned pay of the son who is on active service overseas to maintain herself?
Did my hon. friend say, is it the intention? The assigned pay which is the basis of the allowance would be available for her to use.
Must she use it?
If she does not need it, I suppose not.
Take the case of a father receiving only $5 and the son assigning $20 or $25 of his pay. Would it be necessary for the mother to use that $25 for her keep?
I do not understand what my hon. friend means when he says, "Would it be necessary." If she had no other money, of course it would be necessary.

That is exactly the point. I imagine the dependents' allowance board would take this view: If the father is earning $5 or $20 a month as janitor and the mother is getting $25 assigned pay, that amounts to $45 a month and she does not need any more. What I want to know is, would they be expected to use that assigned pay in order to maintain them? Would it be counted as income, or should they rightfully be entitled to consideration for mothers' allowances?
I understand from the chairman of the dependents' board of trustees that she is allowed $40 a month as income excluding assigned pay, without affecting her right to dependents' allowances.

The ruling I got from the allowance board was this: Where assigned pay is paid with dependents' allowance, the assigned pay is counted as income. When assigned pay is paid without an allowance, then it is not. I had in mind this case. The father is getting old age pension. They have three sons in the army. Each of the sons is assigning $20 a month. One of the sons gets dependents' allowance for his mother. That gives her a total income, assigned pay of one soldier plus dependent's allowance of $540. She is allowed only $365; therefore, the old age pension is
reduced by the difference between $365 and $540. That is different from the attitude taken in the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Under that act the board do not take into consideration assigned pay. This woman is investing the total amount of the assigned pay in bonds in the names of her sons, so that they will have that money on their return. I think in that case the assigned pay should not be taken into consideration at all. The dependents' allowance only should be taken into consideration; then there would be no need to reduce the amount of the old age pension. I do not think the assigned pay should be taken into consideration when it is being invested in bonds for the sons on their return.

I note what my hon. friend has said and we shall deal with it to-morrow. If the committee is agreeable I should like to move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

To-morrow we shall continue with the discussion of the war appropriations. Before adjournment to-morrow we shall probably ask to be allowed to put in two additional departments.
Wait a minute.
Post Office and Pensions.
What do you want two more for now?

In case some minister may not be present.
Business of the House

We have two departments in to-night in the last five minutes. After all, members of the house have few opportunities of raising matters concerning their constituencies, and it seems to me to get the departments in, in this way, as was done last year, and then call the remainder in the last few days of the session, is unfair to the members, and I object to putting too many departments in supply at this stage. We have two in now and that should be sufficient to give us work on Fridays.

I think the Prime Minister
indicated this afternoon that we hope to get the estimates discussed on Fridays.
That is right.

We have only two departments in. It might happen that the ministers of these departments could not be present. I do not think we are infringing on the good nature of the house by asking to be allowed to put in two additional departments tomorrow afternoon.

If that is the case these departments should not be brought in during the last two or three minutes at night, but early in the day; otherwise we shall be compelled to raise some matter and block the going into supply of so many of the departments.

That is a matter which my hon. friend can bring up to-morrow if he wishes. This is the procedure which has been followed in the past, and I draw the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that there is still a very considerable number of departments to be brought in, as my hon. friend knows.

We were told that last year, and at the end of the session all of the departments went in at once and we had not an opportunity to do the things we wanted to do. Moreover, we have no private members' days this year.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
